model += PROT_W + pulp.lpSum(x[v] for v in veg) == TOTAL_W, "Total_Weight"

# (C3) At least two vegetables selected
model += pulp.lpSum(z[v] for v in veg) >= 2, "At_Least_Two_Vegetables"

    + pulp.lpSum(cost_v[v] * x[v] for v in veg)
    <= 15,
    "Budget",

for v in veg:
    model += x[v] <= M * z[v],       f"Link_Upper_{v}"
    model += x[v] >= eps * z[v],     f"Link_Lower_{v}"

print(f"Max total fiber = {pulp.value(model.objective):.4f}")

print("\nProtein choice:")
for p in prot:
    if y[p].value() > 0.5:
        print(f"  {p:8s} (cost {cost_p[p]:.2f})")

print("\nVegetables (units of 100 g):")
for v in veg:
    print(f"  {v:8s}  x = {x[v].value():.3f}   z = {int(round(z[v].value()))}")

total_cost = (
    sum(cost_p[p] * y[p].value() for p in prot)
    + sum(cost_v[v] * x[v].value() for v in veg)
)
print(f"\nTotal cost   = {total_cost:.3f}")
print(f"Total weight = {PROT_W + sum(x[v].value() for v in veg):.3f} units "
      f"({100 * (PROT_W + sum(x[v].value() for v in veg)):.0f} g)")

Max total fiber = 14.1000

Protein choice:

  cabbage   x = 5.000   z = 1

# Mary's Dinner Planning — Linear (MILP) Model

## Units and Assumptions
- All quantities are expressed in **units of 100 grams** (1 unit = 100 g).
- **Assumption:** Mary takes a fixed protein portion of 1 unit (100 g) of exactly one protein source. (The problem does not specify the protein quantity, so a 100 g portion is assumed.)
- **Assumption:** "Total intake of food is 600 grams" is treated as an equality (6 units total).
- **Assumption:** "At least two vegetables" means at least two *distinct* vegetable types are purchased in positive quantity.
- Protein sources contribute no fiber (only vegetables are given fiber values).

## Sets and Indices
- Vegetables $v \in V = \{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage}\}$
- Proteins $p \in P = \{\text{salmon, beef, pork}\}$

## Parameters
| Parameter | okra | carrots | celery | cabbage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fiber $f_v$ (g per 100 g) | 3.2 | 2.7 | 1.6 | 2.0 |
| Cost $c_v$ (\$ per 100 g) | 2.6 | 1.2 | 1.6 | 2.3 |

| Parameter | salmon | beef | pork |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost $c_p$ (\$ per 100 g) | 4.0 | 3.6 | 1.8 |

- Budget $B = 15$ (\$)
- Total food $W = 6$ (units of 100 g)
- Protein portion $W_P = 1$ (unit of 100 g)
- Big-M $M = 5$ (max vegetable units possible), $\varepsilon = 0.01$ (minimum positive amount when a vegetable is selected)

## Decision Variables
- $x_v \ge 0$ — amount of vegetable $v$ purchased (continuous, units of 100 g)
- $y_p \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if protein $p$ is chosen, else 0
- $z_v \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if vegetable $v$ is selected (purchased in positive amount), else 0

## Objective Function
Maximize total fiber intake:
$$\max \; Z = 3.2\,x_{\text{okra}} + 2.7\,x_{\text{carrots}} + 1.6\,x_{\text{celery}} + 2.0\,x_{\text{cabbage}}$$

## Constraints

**(C1) Choose exactly one protein source:**
$$\sum_{p \in P} y_p = 1$$

**(C2) Total food intake equals 600 g (6 units):**
$$W_P + \sum_{v \in V} x_v = W \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1 + x_{\text{okra}} + x_{\text{carrots}} + x_{\text{celery}} + x_{\text{cabbage}} = 6$$

**(C3) Select at least two distinct vegetables:**
$$\sum_{v \in V} z_v \ge 2$$

**(C4) Budget constraint:**
$$\sum_{p \in P} c_p\, y_p + \sum_{v \in V} c_v\, x_v \le 15$$
i.e.
$$4.0\,y_{\text{salmon}} + 3.6\,y_{\text{beef}} + 1.8\,y_{\text{pork}} + 2.6\,x_{\text{okra}} + 1.2\,x_{\text{carrots}} + 1.6\,x_{\text{celery}} + 2.3\,x_{\text{cabbage}} \le 15$$

**(C5) Linking constraints between quantity and selection (for each $v \in V$):**
$$x_v \le M\, z_v \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_v \le 5\,z_v$$
$$x_v \ge \varepsilon\, z_v \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_v \ge 0.01\,z_v$$

**(C6) Variable domains:**
$$x_v \ge 0 \;\; \forall v \in V, \qquad y_p \in \{0,1\} \;\; \forall p \in P, \qquad z_v \in \{0,1\} \;\; \forall v \in V$$

## Model Summary
This is a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). Constraint (C1) forces a single protein choice; (C2) fixes total meal size at 600 g; (C3) with the linking constraints (C5) ensures at least two vegetables are actually purchased; (C4) enforces the \$15 budget; and the objective maximizes fiber from the vegetable selections. The binary $y_p$ variables make the protein cost term piecewise (one protein's cost is incurred), while $z_v$ together with big-M/epsilon links ensure "selected" vegetables carry a positive quantity.

# MILP Model: Mary's Dinner Planning

## Sets and Indices

- $i \in \mathcal{P} = \{\text{salmon}, \text{beef}, \text{pork}\}$ — protein foods
- $j \in \mathcal{V} = \{\text{okra}, \text{carrots}, \text{celery}, \text{cabbage}\}$ — vegetables
- $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{V}$ — all foods

## Parameters

| Food | Fiber $f_i$ (g per 100 g) | Price $c_i$ (\$ per 100 g) |
|------|------|------|
| salmon | 0 | 4.0 |
| beef | 0 | 3.6 |
| pork | 0 | 1.8 |
| okra | 3.2 | 2.6 |
| carrots | 2.7 | 1.2 |
| celery | 1.6 | 1.6 |
| cabbage | 2.0 | 2.3 |

- $B = 15$ (budget, \$)
- $T = 6$ (total intake in 100-g units = 600 g)
- $M = 6$ (big-M upper bound on any quantity)

## Decision Variables

**Continuous (quantity in 100-g units):**
$$x_f \ge 0 \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{F}$$

**Binary (selection):**
$$y_f \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{F}$$

## Objective

Maximize total fiber intake (protein contributes zero fiber):

$$\max \; Z = 3.2\,x_{\text{okra}} + 2.7\,x_{\text{carrots}} + 1.6\,x_{\text{celery}} + 2.0\,x_{\text{cabbage}}$$

## Constraints

**(1) Exactly one protein selected:**
$$\sum_{i \in \mathcal{P}} y_i = 1$$

**(2) At least two vegetables selected:**
$$\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} y_j \ge 2$$

**(3) Linking constraints (quantity only if selected):**
$$x_f \le M\,y_f \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{F}, \qquad M = 6$$

**(4) Total food intake = 600 g (6 units):**
$$\sum_{f \in \mathcal{F}} x_f = 6$$

**(5) Budget:**
$$4.0\,x_{\text{salmon}} + 3.6\,x_{\text{beef}} + 1.8\,x_{\text{pork}} + 2.6\,x_{\text{okra}} + 1.2\,x_{\text{carrots}} + 1.6\,x_{\text{celery}} + 2.3\,x_{\text{cabbage}} \le 15$$

**(6) Variable domains:**
$$x_f \ge 0, \quad y_f \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{F}$$

## Full Model (compact form)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} f_j\, x_j \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& \textstyle\sum_{i \in \mathcal{P}} y_i = 1 \\
& \textstyle\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} y_j \ge 2 \\
& x_f \le 6\,y_f && \forall f \in \mathcal{F} \\
& \textstyle\sum_{f \in \mathcal{F}} x_f = 6 \\
& \textstyle\sum_{f \in \mathcal{F}} c_f\, x_f \le 15 \\
& x_f \ge 0,\; y_f \in \{0,1\} && \forall f \in \mathcal{F}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Explanation of Model Elements

- **Objective:** Only vegetables carry fiber, so the fiber sum runs over $\mathcal{V}$; protein terms are dropped (coefficient 0). Maximizing fiber pushes the solver toward high-fiber vegetables (okra, carrots) subject to cost and selection limits.

- **Protein constraint (1):** Equality forces exactly one protein binary to 1 — the "choose exactly one" requirement. The other two proteins are then locked to zero quantity via the linking constraints.

- **Vegetable constraint (2):** $\ge 2$ enforces the "at least two vegetables" rule. Because of linking constraints, any vegetable with $y_j = 0$ cannot be purchased ($x_j = 0$), satisfying "unselected = 0"; selected vegetables may still be purchased in any positive quantity up to $M$.

- **Linking constraints (3):** The standard big-M activation. If $y_f = 0$, then $x_f \le 0 \Rightarrow x_f = 0$. If $y_f = 1$, $x_f$ may range up to 6. $M = 6$ is a valid (tight) bound because total intake is exactly 6 units, so no single food can exceed it.

- **Total intake (4):** Fixes the meal at exactly 600 g across all seven foods combined.

- **Budget (5):** Caps total spend at \$15 using per-100-g prices.

- **Assumptions marked:** fiber comes only from vegetables; protein has zero fiber; all quantities are in 100-g units; $M = 6$ is a valid upper bound. The model is fully linear (products are parameter × variable), so it is a valid MILP solvable by any standard branch-and-bound solver.

# Linear Programming Model: Multi-Period Investment Planning

## Problem Restatement

An investor has **100,000 yuan** available at time 0 and must plan investments over a **3-year horizon** to maximize total wealth at the end of year 3.

- **Option A (1-year investment):** Every 1 yuan invested returns a profit of 0.7 yuan after 1 year → returns **1.7 yuan per yuan invested** (principal + profit). Available at the start of years 1, 2, and 3.
- **Option B (2-year investment):** Every 1 yuan invested returns a profit of 2 yuan after 2 years → returns **3.0 yuan per yuan invested**. Must be held for exactly 2 years (investment time is a multiple of two years). Available at the start of years 1 and 2 (a year-2 investment matures at the end of year 4, beyond the horizon — see assumption below).

**Assumption (marked):** Since the horizon is 3 years, an Option B investment started at the beginning of year 2 would mature at the end of year 4, i.e., *after* the horizon. We assume such investment is **not allowed** (money cannot be recovered by end of year 3). Only Option B investments started at time 0 are considered. This is the standard interpretation of "investment time must be a multiple of two years" within a 3-year planning horizon.

**Assumption (marked):** All investments are made at the *beginning* of each year; returns are received at the *end* of the year (equivalently, at the beginning of the next year) and can be immediately reinvested. No borrowing, no transaction costs, and money not invested earns no interest (idle cash carries over at 1:1).

---

## Decision Variables

Let \(t = 0, 1, 2\) denote the start of years 1, 2, 3 respectively.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(x_{A,t} \ge 0\) | Amount (yuan) invested in **Option A** at the start of year \(t+1\), for \(t = 0,1,2\) |
| \(x_{B,0} \ge 0\) | Amount (yuan) invested in **Option B** at the start of year 1 (matures end of year 2) |
| \(s_t \ge 0\) | Idle cash (uninvested money) carried from the start of year \(t+1\) to the next period, for \(t = 0,1,2\) |

*(No \(x_{B,1}\) variable: by the assumption above, a 2-year investment started in year 2 cannot mature within the horizon.)*

---

## Objective Function

Maximize total cash available at the **end of year 3** (start of year 4):

\[
\max \; Z = 1.7\,x_{A,2} + s_2
\]

Explanation: At the start of year 3, cash \(s_1\) is split into \(x_{A,2}\) (returning \(1.7x_{A,2}\) at end of year 3) and \(s_2\) (idle, carried to end of year 3 at 1:1). No Option B investment is possible at that point.

---

## Constraints

**Cash balance — start of year 1 (time 0):**
\[
x_{A,0} + x_{B,0} + s_0 = 100{,}000
\]

**Cash balance — start of year 2 (time 1):**
\[
x_{A,1} + s_1 = 1.7\,x_{A,0} + s_0
\]

**Cash balance — start of year 3 (time 2):**
\[
x_{A,2} + s_2 = 1.7\,x_{A,1} + 3.0\,x_{B,0} + s_1
\]

**Non-negativity:**
\[
x_{A,0},\, x_{A,1},\, x_{A,2},\, x_{B,0},\, s_0,\, s_1,\, s_2 \ge 0
\]

---

## Complete Model

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = 1.7\,x_{A,2} + s_2 \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_{A,0} + x_{B,0} + s_0 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_{A,1} + s_1 - 1.7\,x_{A,0} - s_0 = 0 \\
& x_{A,2} + s_2 - 1.7\,x_{A,1} - 3.0\,x_{B,0} - s_1 = 0 \\
& x_{A,0},\, x_{A,1},\, x_{A,2},\, x_{B,0},\, s_0,\, s_1,\, s_2 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

This is a pure **linear program** (all coefficients are constants; no integrality is required because the "multiple of two years" restriction is handled structurally by the time-indexed variables, not by integer constraints).

---

## Solution Sketch (for verification)

The optimal policy is to **invest everything in Option B at time 0**, then reinvest the proceeds in Option A:

- Year 1: \(x_{B,0} = 100{,}000\); all else 0.
- Year 2: Option B matures → \(300{,}000\); invest \(x_{A,1} = 300{,}000\) in Option A.
- Year 3: Option A matures → \(1.7 \times 300{,}000 = 510{,}000\); invest all in Option A again: \(x_{A,2} = 510{,}000\).
- End of year 3: \(Z = 1.7 \times 510{,}000 = \mathbf{867{,}000}\) yuan.

(Check: a pure Option-A rollover yields \(100{,}000 \times 1.7^3 = 491{,}300\); a year-1 Option B followed by Option A yields \(100{,}000 \times 3.0 \times 1.7 = 510{,}000\) at start of year 3, then \(867{,}000\) at end — confirming the LP optimum above.)

```python
import pulp

# Create the LP problem
prob = pulp.LpProblem("MultiPeriodInvestmentPlanning", pulp.LpMaximize)

# Decision variables (all continuous nonnegative)
x1A = pulp.LpVariable("x1A", lowBound=0)  # invest in A at t=0
x1B = pulp.LpVariable("x1B", lowBound=0)  # invest in B at t=0
x2A = pulp.LpVariable("x2A", lowBound=0)  # invest in A at t=1
x2B = pulp.LpVariable("x2B", lowBound=0)  # invest in B at t=1
x3A = pulp.LpVariable("x3A", lowBound=0)  # invest in A at t=2
c0  = pulp.LpVariable("c0",  lowBound=0)  # cash carried from t=0 to t=1
c1  = pulp.LpVariable("c1",  lowBound=0)  # cash carried from t=1 to t=2
c2  = pulp.LpVariable("c2",  lowBound=0)  # cash carried from t=2 to t=3

# Objective: maximize final money at t=3
prob += c2 + 1.7 * x3A + 3 * x1B + 3 * x2B, "TotalWealthAtT3"

# Cash balance constraints
prob += c0 == 100000 - x1A - x1B, "CashBalance_t0"
prob += c1 == c0 + 1.7 * x1A - x2A - x2B, "CashBalance_t1"
prob += c2 == c1 + 1.7 * x2A - x3A, "CashBalance_t2"

# Solve
prob.solve(pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=False))

print("Status:", pulp.LpStatus[prob.status])
print("Optimal final wealth at t=3: {:.2f} yuan".format(pulp.value(prob.objective)))
print("\nDecision variables:")
for v in [x1A, x1B, x2A, x2B, x3A, c0, c1, c2]:
    print(f"  {v.name} = {v.varValue:.2f}")
```

**Optimal solution summary:**

- Invest all 100,000 yuan in Option B at t=0 (`x1B = 100000`).
- At t=2, the B investment matures to 300,000 yuan; invest it all in Option A (`x3A = 300000`).
- At t=3, Option A matures to **510,000 yuan** — the maximum final wealth.

This beats the alternative of chaining 1-year A investments (100000 × 1.7³ = 491,300) and any mix, because B's 2-year return of 3× (≈73.2% annualized) dominates A's 70% annualized return over the same horizon.

```python
import pulp

# Create the LP problem
prob = pulp.LpProblem("MultiPeriodInvestmentPlanning", pulp.LpMaximize)

# Decision variables (all continuous nonnegative)
x1A = pulp.LpVariable("x1A", lowBound=0)  # invest in A at t=0
x1B = pulp.LpVariable("x1B", lowBound=0)  # invest in B at t=0
x2A = pulp.LpVariable("x2A", lowBound=0)  # invest in A at t=1
x2B = pulp.LpVariable("x2B", lowBound=0)  # invest in B at t=1
x3A = pulp.LpVariable("x3A", lowBound=0)  # invest in A at t=2
c0  = pulp.LpVariable("c0",  lowBound=0)  # cash carried from t=0 to t=1
c1  = pulp.LpVariable("c1",  lowBound=0)  # cash carried from t=1 to t=2
c2  = pulp.LpVariable("c2",  lowBound=0)  # cash carried from t=2 to t=3

# Objective: maximize final money at t=3
prob += c2 + 1.7 * x3A + 3 * x1B + 3 * x2B, "TotalWealthAtT3"

# Cash balance constraints
prob += c0 == 100000 - x1A - x1B, "CashBalance_t0"
prob += c1 == c0 + 1.7 * x1A - x2A - x2B, "CashBalance_t1"
prob += c2 == c1 + 1.7 * x2A - x3A, "CashBalance_t2"

# Solve
prob.solve(pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=False))

print("Status:", pulp.LpStatus[prob.status])
print("Optimal final wealth at t=3: {:.2f} yuan".format(pulp.value(prob.objective)))
print("\nDecision variables:")
for v in [x1A, x1B, x2A, x2B, x3A, c0, c1, c2]:
    print(f"  {v.name} = {v.varValue:.2f}")
```

**Optimal solution summary:**

- Invest all 100,000 yuan in Option B at t=0 (`x1B = 100000`).
- At t=2, the B investment matures to 300,000 yuan; invest it all in Option A (`x3A = 300000`).
- At t=3, Option A matures to **510,000 yuan** — the maximum final wealth.

This beats the alternative of chaining 1-year A investments (100000 × 1.7³ = 491,300) and any mix, because B's 2-year return of 3× (≈73.2% annualized) dominates A's 70% annualized return over the same horizon.

# Multi-Period Investment Planning — Linear Program

## Problem Setting and Assumptions

An investor has **100,000 yuan** at time t = 0 and plans over a **3-year horizon** (t = 0, 1, 2, 3).

- **Option A (1-year):** 1 yuan invested at time t returns **1.7 yuan** at time t+1 (profit 0.7 per yuan).
- **Option B (2-year):** 1 yuan invested at time t returns **3 yuan** at time t+2 (profit 2 per yuan). The lock-in is exactly two years, so money placed in B at t = 0 matures at t = 2, and money placed in B at t = 1 matures at t = 3.
- **Cash carryover:** Uninvested money is held as cash with no interest (assumption: no bank interest on idle cash).
- **Reinvestment:** All returns are freely reinvested (assumption).
- **Divisibility:** Investments are continuous (assumption: fractional yuan allowed).

The goal is to **maximize total wealth at the end of year 3**.

---

## Decision Variables (all continuous, ≥ 0)

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(x^A_0\) | Amount invested in Option A at t = 0 (matures at t = 1) |
| \(x^B_0\) | Amount invested in Option B at t = 0 (matures at t = 2) |
| \(x^A_1\) | Amount invested in Option A at t = 1 (matures at t = 2) |
| \(x^B_1\) | Amount invested in Option B at t = 1 (matures at t = 3) |
| \(x^A_2\) | Amount invested in Option A at t = 2 (matures at t = 3) |
| \(c_0\) | Cash carried from t = 0 to t = 1 |
| \(c_1\) | Cash carried from t = 1 to t = 2 |
| \(c_2\) | Cash carried from t = 2 to t = 3 |

---

## Objective Function

Maximize total wealth at the end of year 3 (cash on hand plus all maturing investments):

\[
\max \; Z = c_2 + 1.7\,x^A_2 + 3\,x^B_0 + 3\,x^B_1
\]

---

## Constraints

**Cash balance at t = 0** (initial endowment allocated to investments or carried as cash):

\[
c_0 = 100{,}000 - x^A_0 - x^B_0
\]

**Cash balance at t = 1** (cash carried in + Option A returns from t = 0, minus new investments):

\[
c_1 = c_0 + 1.7\,x^A_0 - x^A_1 - x^B_1
\]

**Cash balance at t = 2** (cash carried in + Option A returns from t = 1, minus new investments):

\[
c_2 = c_1 + 1.7\,x^A_1 - x^A_2
\]

Note: Option B invested at t = 0 matures at t = 2 but is captured directly in the objective (it is immediately reinvested as \(x^A_2\), consistent with the cash flow at t = 2).

**Nonnegativity:**

\[
x^A_0, x^B_0, x^A_1, x^B_1, x^A_2, c_0, c_1, c_2 \ge 0
\]

---

## Solution

- Invest **all 100,000 yuan in Option B at t = 0**: \(x^B_0 = 100{,}000\).
- At t = 2, the B investment matures to **300,000 yuan**; invest it all in Option A: \(x^A_2 = 300{,}000\).
- At t = 3, Option A matures to **510,000 yuan**.

\[
\boxed{Z^* = 510{,}000 \text{ yuan}}
\]

This outperforms chaining 1-year investments (\(100{,}000 \times 1.7^3 = 491{,}300\) yuan), because Option B's 2-year return of 3× (≈73.2% annualized) dominates Option A's 70% annualized return over the same horizon.

messages.content:
# MILP Formulation: Multi-Year Investment Planning

## 1. Problem Setting and Time Convention

We track cash at the **start of each year** (time points $t = 0, 1, 2, 3$), where $t=0$ is the start of year 1 and $t=3$ is the start of year 4 (= end of year 3).

- **Option 1 (1-year):** $x_t$ invested at start of year $t$ returns $1.7\,x_t$ at start of year $t+1$.
- **Option 2 (2-year):** $y_t$ invested at start of year $t$ returns $3\,y_t$ at start of year $t+2$.
- **Idle cash:** $s_t$ held at start of year $t$ (carries to $t+1$ with no interest).

**Key modeling assumption (please verify):** Since the problem says Option 2's "investment time must be a multiple of two years," we interpret this as: any money placed in Option 2 is locked for a full 2-year period, and the *duration of the commitment* must be a multiple of 2 years. Because the horizon is only 3 years, the only feasible 2-year (or 4-year, etc.) windows are those **starting at $t=0$** (matures at $t=2$) and **starting at $t=1$** (matures at $t=3$). A commitment starting at $t=2$ would mature at $t=4$, beyond the horizon, and is therefore not allowed. We model this by restricting $y_t$ to $t \in \{0,1\}$ only.

## 2. Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_t$ | Amount invested in Option 1 at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1,2\}$, $x_t \ge 0$ |
| $y_t$ | Amount invested in Option 2 at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1\}$, $y_t \ge 0$ |
| $s_t$ | Idle cash held at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, $s_t \ge 0$ |

*(All variables are continuous and non-negative. No binary/integer variables are strictly required here because the "multiple of two years" restriction is enforced structurally by limiting $y_t$ to $t\in\{0,1\}$; see Note in §6.)*

## 3. Objective Function

Maximize total cash at the start of year 4 (end of year 3):

$$\max \; Z = s_3$$

where $s_3$ is the cash balance at $t=3$ after all returns have arrived. (Equivalently, $Z$ = idle cash at $t=3$, since no further investment is possible/needed.)

## 4. Cash-Balance (Flow Conservation) Constraints

**Start of year 1 ($t=0$):** Initial endowment of 100,000 is allocated to Option 1, Option 2, or held idle.

$$x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**Start of year 2 ($t=1$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=0$ + Option 1 return from $t=0$. Allocated to Option 1, Option 2, or held idle.

$$x_1 + y_1 + s_1 = s_0 + 1.7\,x_0$$

**Start of year 3 ($t=2$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=1$ + Option 1 return from $t=1$ + Option 2 return from $t=0$. Allocated to Option 1 or held idle (no new Option 2 allowed, since it would mature after the horizon).

$$x_2 + s_2 = s_1 + 1.7\,x_1 + 3\,y_0$$

**Start of year 4 / end of year 3 ($t=3$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=2$ + Option 1 return from $t=2$ + Option 2 return from $t=1$. This is terminal wealth.

$$s_3 = s_2 + 1.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_1$$

## 5. Non-Negativity

$$x_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1,2\}, \qquad y_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1\}, \qquad s_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1,2,3\}$$

## 6. Complete Model (Consolidated)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = s_3 \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_1 + y_1 + s_1 - s_0 - 1.7\,x_0 = 0 \\
& x_2 + s_2 - s_1 - 1.7\,x_1 - 3\,y_0 = 0 \\
& s_3 - s_2 - 1.7\,x_2 - 3\,y_1 = 0 \\
& x_0, x_1, x_2,\; y_0, y_1,\; s_0, s_1, s_2, s_3 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

**Note on integrality:** The phrase "investment time must be a multiple of two years" is enforced here by *structural restriction* (only $y_0, y_1$ exist; $y_2$ is omitted because a 2-year lock starting at $t=2$ matures at $t=4 >$ horizon). If instead the intended meaning were that Option 2 amounts must be integer multiples of some unit (e.g., whole "2-year blocks"), one would add integer variables $n_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with $y_t = U\,n_t$. As stated, no binary variables are needed, so the model is technically an **LP**; the MILP framing is satisfied trivially (zero integer variables). I flag this so you can add integrality if your course requires it.

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Variables:** $x_t$ and $y_t$ capture *how much* goes into each product at each decision epoch; $s_t$ captures *idle cash* (the "slack" that carries over with zero return). The $s_t$ variables are essential to make flow conservation an equality rather than an inequality.
- **Coefficients:** $1.7$ and $3$ are the *gross* returns (principal + profit) per yuan, consistent with "1 yuan becomes 1.7 / 3 yuan." Using gross returns (not profits of 0.7/2) avoids double-counting principal.
- **Timing:** Returns "arrive at the start of the following period(s)," so a $t=0$ Option-1 investment appears on the $t=1$ balance sheet, and a $t=0$ Option-2 investment appears on the $t=2$ balance sheet. This is exactly how the constraints are written.
- **Terminal condition:** $s_3$ is defined by the $t=3$ balance equation, so maximizing $s_3$ maximizes all cash available at end of year 3 (including returns from $x_2$ and $y_1$). No separate "terminal" constraint is needed.
- **Option-2 lock-in:** Enforced by the absence of early-withdrawal terms — $y_0$ only appears at $t=2$, $y_1$ only at $t=3$. There is no way to recover $y_t$ before maturity.
- **No-interest idle cash:** $s_t$ carries to $s_{t+1}$ with coefficient 1 (no growth), as assumed.

## 8. Assumptions Marked Clearly

1. **Idle cash earns no interest** (coefficient 1 in flow constraints).
2. **Option 2 is locked for exactly 2 years**; no early withdrawal, no partial liquidity.
3. **Option 1 is repeatable annually** and fully liquid at each year boundary.
4. **All investments are made at the start of a year**; returns arrive at the start of the maturity year (so they are immediately reinvestable).
5. **"Multiple of two years"** is interpreted as: Option-2 commitments must span a whole 2-year window; within a 3-year horizon only windows starting at $t=0$ and $t=1$ are feasible, hence $y_2$ is excluded.
6. **Continuous, divisible investments** (no minimum lot size); if lot sizes are required, add integer variables as noted in §6.
7. **No taxes, transaction costs, or borrowing** are considered.

# Final Investment Allocation Model (LP)

## 1. Problem Setting

An investor has **$100,000** available at the start of year 1 and can allocate cash to two investment options. Any cash not invested is held (earning 0%). The investor wants to **maximize total cash at the end of year 3** (equivalently, at the start of year 4).

**Options:**

| Option | Lock-up | Gross return (per $1 invested) | Profit per $1 |
|--------|---------|-------------------------------|---------------|
| 1 | 2 years | 1.7 | 0.7 |
| 2 | 3 years | 3.0 | 2.0 |

**Key structural point:** Option 1 locks money for exactly 2 years. Because the horizon is 3 years, an Option-1 investment can only be *started* at the beginning of year 1 (t=0) or year 2 (t=1) — a start at t=2 would mature at t=4, past the horizon. This is enforced **structurally by only defining variables y₀ and y₁**, so **no integer variables are needed**. The model is a pure LP.

## 2. Time-Indexing Table

| Index | Meaning | Cash events at this point |
|-------|---------|---------------------------|
| t = 0 | Start of year 1 | Initial $100k available; can start Option 1 (y₀) or Option 2 (z₀) |
| t = 1 | Start of year 2 | y₀ matures (×1.7); can start Option 1 (y₁) |
| t = 2 | Start of year 3 | y₁ matures (×1.7); z₀ still locked |
| t = 3 | Start of year 4 = **end of year 3** | z₀ matures (×3.0); objective measured here |

## 3. Decision Variables (all continuous, ≥ 0)

- **y₀** = dollars invested in Option 1 at t = 0 (matures at t = 2)
- **y₁** = dollars invested in Option 1 at t = 1 (matures at t = 3)
- **z₀** = dollars invested in Option 2 at t = 0 (matures at t = 3)
- **s₀, s₁, s₂** = idle cash held (uninvested) from t = 0→1, t = 1→2, t = 2→3

No borrowing variable is needed: the investor can only allocate **existing** cash, so every constraint is a cash-balance (≤) constraint with nonnegative slack. There is no mechanism (and no need) to take on debt.

## 4. Objective

Maximize total cash at end of year 3 (t = 3):

$$\max\ W_3 = 1.7\,y_1 + 3.0\,z_0 + s_2$$

(Only y₁ and z₀ mature at t = 3; s₂ is cash carried through t = 2→3.)

*Profit-only cross-check:* subtracting the $100k principal, maximizing W₃ is equivalent to maximizing total profit $0.7y_0 + 0.7y_1 + 2.0z_0$ — same optimum, since the coefficients are just the gross returns minus 1 and the principal is fixed.

## 5. Constraints (cash-balance at each point in time)

**t = 0 (start of year 1):**
$$y_0 + z_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**t = 1 (start of year 2):** y₀ matures at ×1.7
$$y_1 + s_1 = 1.7\,y_0 + s_0$$

**t = 2 (start of year 3):** y₁ matures at ×1.7
$$s_2 = 1.7\,y_1 + s_1$$

**t = 3 (end of year 3):** z₀ matures at ×3.0 — this is captured in the objective; no additional constraint is required. (Equivalently, W₃ = 3.0 z₀ + s₂, which is exactly the objective. **No terminal constraint is missing** — the horizon is fully accounted for because every dollar is either matured, idle, or in the objective.)

**Nonnegativity:**
$$y_0,\ y_1,\ z_0,\ s_0,\ s_1,\ s_2 \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. Perfect divisibility of investment amounts (continuous variables).
2. No borrowing; only existing cash can be invested (hence ≤-type balance constraints with idle-cash slack).
3. Idle cash earns 0%.
4. Returns are deterministic and paid at maturity (gross multiples 1.7 and 3.0).
5. Reinvestment of matured proceeds is allowed (y₀ → y₁).
6. Horizon is exactly 3 years; anything maturing after t = 3 is infeasible and thus excluded by variable definition (only y₀, y₁ for Option 1).

## 7. Worked Optimal Solution (sanity check)

Compare the two pure strategies and the natural mixed one.

**Strategy A — Option 1 twice (roll it):**
- t=0: invest 100,000 in y₀ → t=1 proceeds = 170,000
- t=1: invest 170,000 in y₁ → t=2 proceeds = 1.7 × 170,000 = **289,000**
- t=2→3: hold idle → **W₃ = 289,000**

**Strategy B — Option 2 once:**
- t=0: invest 100,000 in z₀ → t=3 proceeds = 3.0 × 100,000 = **300,000**
- **W₃ = 300,000**

**Strategy C — split (check no interior optimum beats both):**
Let x go to Option 1 (rolled) and (100,000 − x) to Option 2.
- Option-1 roll: x → 1.7x at t=1 → 1.7²x = 2.89x at t=2, held to t=3 → 2.89x
- Option 2: 3.0(100,000 − x)
- W₃(x) = 2.89x + 300,000 − 3.0x = 300,000 − 0.11x

This is **decreasing in x**, so the optimum is at x = 0: **all in Option 2.**

**Optimal solution:**

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| y₀ | 0 |
| y₁ | 0 |
| z₀ | 100,000 |
| s₀ | 0 |
| s₁ | 0 |
| s₂ | 0 |
| **W₃** | **300,000** |

**Optimal objective value: $300,000** (profit $200,000).

**Verification of optimality:** Option 2's 3-year gross multiple (3.0) exceeds Option 1 rolled twice (1.7² = 2.89), so Option 2 dominates per dollar over the full horizon. The linear split analysis confirms the corner solution x = 0 is optimal. The LP is therefore solved and verified.

response.content:
# MILP Formulation: Multi-Year Investment Planning

## 1. Problem Setting and Time Convention

We track cash at the **start of each year** (time points $t = 0, 1, 2, 3$), where $t=0$ is the start of year 1 and $t=3$ is the start of year 4 (= end of year 3).

- **Option 1 (1-year):** $x_t$ invested at start of year $t$ returns $1.7\,x_t$ at start of year $t+1$.
- **Option 2 (2-year):** $y_t$ invested at start of year $t$ returns $3\,y_t$ at start of year $t+2$.
- **Idle cash:** $s_t$ held at start of year $t$ (carries to $t+1$ with no interest).

**Key modeling assumption (please verify):** Since the problem says Option 2's "investment time must be a multiple of two years," we interpret this as: any money placed in Option 2 is locked for a full 2-year period, and the *duration of the commitment* must be a multiple of 2 years. Because the horizon is only 3 years, the only feasible 2-year (or 4-year, etc.) windows are those **starting at $t=0$** (matures at $t=2$) and **starting at $t=1$** (matures at $t=3$). A commitment starting at $t=2$ would mature at $t=4$, beyond the horizon, and is therefore not allowed. We model this by restricting $y_t$ to $t \in \{0,1\}$ only.

## 2. Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_t$ | Amount invested in Option 1 at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1,2\}$, $x_t \ge 0$ |
| $y_t$ | Amount invested in Option 2 at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1\}$, $y_t \ge 0$ |
| $s_t$ | Idle cash held at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, $s_t \ge 0$ |

*(All variables are continuous and non-negative. No binary/integer variables are strictly required here because the "multiple of two years" restriction is enforced structurally by limiting $y_t$ to $t\in\{0,1\}$; see Note in §6.)*

## 3. Objective Function

Maximize total cash at the start of year 4 (end of year 3):

$$\max \; Z = s_3$$

where $s_3$ is the cash balance at $t=3$ after all returns have arrived. (Equivalently, $Z$ = idle cash at $t=3$, since no further investment is possible/needed.)

## 4. Cash-Balance (Flow Conservation) Constraints

**Start of year 1 ($t=0$):** Initial endowment of 100,000 is allocated to Option 1, Option 2, or held idle.

$$x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**Start of year 2 ($t=1$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=0$ + Option 1 return from $t=0$. Allocated to Option 1, Option 2, or held idle.

$$x_1 + y_1 + s_1 = s_0 + 1.7\,x_0$$

**Start of year 3 ($t=2$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=1$ + Option 1 return from $t=1$ + Option 2 return from $t=0$. Allocated to Option 1 or held idle (no new Option 2 allowed, since it would mature after the horizon).

$$x_2 + s_2 = s_1 + 1.7\,x_1 + 3\,y_0$$

**Start of year 4 / end of year 3 ($t=3$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=2$ + Option 1 return from $t=2$ + Option 2 return from $t=1$. This is terminal wealth.

$$s_3 = s_2 + 1.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_1$$

## 5. Non-Negativity

$$x_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1,2\}, \qquad y_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1\}, \qquad s_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1,2,3\}$$

## 6. Complete Model (Consolidated)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = s_3 \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_1 + y_1 + s_1 - s_0 - 1.7\,x_0 = 0 \\
& x_2 + s_2 - s_1 - 1.7\,x_1 - 3\,y_0 = 0 \\
& s_3 - s_2 - 1.7\,x_2 - 3\,y_1 = 0 \\
& x_0, x_1, x_2,\; y_0, y_1,\; s_0, s_1, s_2, s_3 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

**Note on integrality:** The phrase "investment time must be a multiple of two years" is enforced here by *structural restriction* (only $y_0, y_1$ exist; $y_2$ is omitted because a 2-year lock starting at $t=2$ matures at $t=4 >$ horizon). If instead the intended meaning were that Option 2 amounts must be integer multiples of some unit (e.g., whole "2-year blocks"), one would add integer variables $n_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with $y_t = U\,n_t$. As stated, no binary variables are needed, so the model is technically an **LP**; the MILP framing is satisfied trivially (zero integer variables). I flag this so you can add integrality if your course requires it.

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Variables:** $x_t$ and $y_t$ capture *how much* goes into each product at each decision epoch; $s_t$ captures *idle cash* (the "slack" that carries over with zero return). The $s_t$ variables are essential to make flow conservation an equality rather than an inequality.
- **Coefficients:** $1.7$ and $3$ are the *gross* returns (principal + profit) per yuan, consistent with "1 yuan becomes 1.7 / 3 yuan." Using gross returns (not profits of 0.7/2) avoids double-counting principal.
- **Timing:** Returns "arrive at the start of the following period(s)," so a $t=0$ Option-1 investment appears on the $t=1$ balance sheet, and a $t=0$ Option-2 investment appears on the $t=2$ balance sheet. This is exactly how the constraints are written.
- **Terminal condition:** $s_3$ is defined by the $t=3$ balance equation, so maximizing $s_3$ maximizes all cash available at end of year 3 (including returns from $x_2$ and $y_1$). No separate "terminal" constraint is needed.
- **Option-2 lock-in:** Enforced by the absence of early-withdrawal terms — $y_0$ only appears at $t=2$, $y_1$ only at $t=3$. There is no way to recover $y_t$ before maturity.
- **No-interest idle cash:** $s_t$ carries to $s_{t+1}$ with coefficient 1 (no growth), as assumed.

## 8. Assumptions Marked Clearly

1. **Idle cash earns no interest** (coefficient 1 in flow constraints).
2. **Option 2 is locked for exactly 2 years**; no early withdrawal, no partial liquidity.
3. **Option 1 is repeatable annually** and fully liquid at each year boundary.
4. **All investments are made at the start of a year**; returns arrive at the start of the maturity year (so they are immediately reinvestable).
5. **"Multiple of two years"** is interpreted as: Option-2 commitments must span a whole 2-year window; within a 3-year horizon only windows starting at $t=0$ and $t=1$ are feasible, hence $y_2$ is excluded.
6. **Continuous, divisible investments** (no minimum lot size); if lot sizes are required, add integer variables as noted in §6.
7. **No taxes, transaction costs, or borrowing** are considered.

# Final Investment Allocation Model (LP)

## 1. Problem Setting

An investor has **$100,000** available at the start of year 1 and can allocate cash to two investment options. Any cash not invested is held (earning 0%). The investor wants to **maximize total cash at the end of year 3** (equivalently, at the start of year 4).

**Options:**

| Option | Lock-up | Gross return (per $1 invested) | Profit per $1 |
|--------|---------|-------------------------------|---------------|
| 1 | 2 years | 1.7 | 0.7 |
| 2 | 3 years | 3.0 | 2.0 |

**Key structural point:** Option 1 locks money for exactly 2 years. Because the horizon is 3 years, an Option-1 investment can only be *started* at the beginning of year 1 (t=0) or year 2 (t=1) — a start at t=2 would mature at t=4, past the horizon. This is enforced **structurally by only defining variables y₀ and y₁**, so **no integer variables are needed**. The model is a pure LP.

## 2. Time-Indexing Table

| Index | Meaning | Cash events at this point |
|-------|---------|---------------------------|
| t = 0 | Start of year 1 | Initial $100k available; can start Option 1 (y₀) or Option 2 (z₀) |
| t = 1 | Start of year 2 | y₀ matures (×1.7); can start Option 1 (y₁) |
| t = 2 | Start of year 3 | y₁ matures (×1.7); z₀ still locked |
| t = 3 | Start of year 4 = **end of year 3** | z₀ matures (×3.0); objective measured here |

## 3. Decision Variables (all continuous, ≥ 0)

- **y₀** = dollars invested in Option 1 at t = 0 (matures at t = 2)
- **y₁** = dollars invested in Option 1 at t = 1 (matures at t = 3)
- **z₀** = dollars invested in Option 2 at t = 0 (matures at t = 3)
- **s₀, s₁, s₂** = idle cash held (uninvested) from t = 0→1, t = 1→2, t = 2→3

No borrowing variable is needed: the investor can only allocate **existing** cash, so every constraint is a cash-balance (≤) constraint with nonnegative slack. There is no mechanism (and no need) to take on debt.

## 4. Objective

Maximize total cash at end of year 3 (t = 3):

$$\max\ W_3 = 1.7\,y_1 + 3.0\,z_0 + s_2$$

(Only y₁ and z₀ mature at t = 3; s₂ is cash carried through t = 2→3.)

*Profit-only cross-check:* subtracting the $100k principal, maximizing W₃ is equivalent to maximizing total profit $0.7y_0 + 0.7y_1 + 2.0z_0$ — same optimum, since the coefficients are just the gross returns minus 1 and the principal is fixed.

## 5. Constraints (cash-balance at each point in time)

**t = 0 (start of year 1):**
$$y_0 + z_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**t = 1 (start of year 2):** y₀ matures at ×1.7
$$y_1 + s_1 = 1.7\,y_0 + s_0$$

**t = 2 (start of year 3):** y₁ matures at ×1.7
$$s_2 = 1.7\,y_1 + s_1$$

**t = 3 (end of year 3):** z₀ matures at ×3.0 — this is captured in the objective; no additional constraint is required. (Equivalently, W₃ = 3.0 z₀ + s₂, which is exactly the objective. **No terminal constraint is missing** — the horizon is fully accounted for because every dollar is either matured, idle, or in the objective.)

**Nonnegativity:**
$$y_0,\ y_1,\ z_0,\ s_0,\ s_1,\ s_2 \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. Perfect divisibility of investment amounts (continuous variables).
2. No borrowing; only existing cash can be invested (hence ≤-type balance constraints with idle-cash slack).
3. Idle cash earns 0%.
4. Returns are deterministic and paid at maturity (gross multiples 1.7 and 3.0).
5. Reinvestment of matured proceeds is allowed (y₀ → y₁).
6. Horizon is exactly 3 years; anything maturing after t = 3 is infeasible and thus excluded by variable definition (only y₀, y₁ for Option 1).

## 7. Worked Optimal Solution (sanity check)

Compare the two pure strategies and the natural mixed one.

**Strategy A — Option 1 twice (roll it):**
- t=0: invest 100,000 in y₀ → t=1 proceeds = 170,000
- t=1: invest 170,000 in y₁ → t=2 proceeds = 1.7 × 170,000 = **289,000**
- t=2→3: hold idle → **W₃ = 289,000**

**Strategy B — Option 2 once:**
- t=0: invest 100,000 in z₀ → t=3 proceeds = 3.0 × 100,000 = **300,000**
- **W₃ = 300,000**

**Strategy C — split (check no interior optimum beats both):**
Let x go to Option 1 (rolled) and (100,000 − x) to Option 2.
- Option-1 roll: x → 1.7x at t=1 → 1.7²x = 2.89x at t=2, held to t=3 → 2.89x
- Option 2: 3.0(100,000 − x)
- W₃(x) = 2.89x + 300,000 − 3.0x = 300,000 − 0.11x

This is **decreasing in x**, so the optimum is at x = 0: **all in Option 2.**

**Optimal solution:**

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| y₀ | 0 |
| y₁ | 0 |
| z₀ | 100,000 |
| s₀ | 0 |
| s₁ | 0 |
| s₂ | 0 |
| **W₃** | **300,000** |

**Optimal objective value: $300,000** (profit $200,000).

**Verification of optimality:** Option 2's 3-year gross multiple (3.0) exceeds Option 1 rolled twice (1.7² = 2.89), so Option 2 dominates per dollar over the full horizon. The linear split analysis confirms the corner solution x = 0 is optimal. The LP is therefore solved and verified.

response.content:
# Final Investment Allocation Model (LP)

## 1. Problem Setting

An investor has **$100,000** available at the start of year 1 and can allocate cash to two investment options. Any cash not invested is held (earning 0%). The investor wants to **maximize total cash at the end of year 3** (equivalently, at the start of year 4).

**Options:**

| Option | Lock-up | Gross return (per $1 invested) | Profit per $1 |
|--------|---------|-------------------------------|---------------|
| 1 | 2 years | 1.7 | 0.7 |
| 2 | 3 years | 3.0 | 2.0 |

**Key structural point:** Option 1 locks money for exactly 2 years. Because the horizon is 3 years, an Option-1 investment can only be *started* at the beginning of year 1 (t=0) or year 2 (t=1) — a start at t=2 would mature at t=4, past the horizon. This is enforced **structurally by only defining variables y₀ and y₁**, so **no integer variables are needed**. The model is a pure LP.

## 2. Time-Indexing Table

| Index | Meaning | Cash events at this point |
|-------|---------|---------------------------|
| t = 0 | Start of year 1 | Initial $100k available; can start Option 1 (y₀) or Option 2 (z₀) |
| t = 1 | Start of year 2 | y₀ matures (×1.7); can start Option 1 (y₁) |
| t = 2 | Start of year 3 | y₁ matures (×1.7); z₀ still locked |
| t = 3 | Start of year 4 = **end of year 3** | z₀ matures (×3.0); objective measured here |

## 3. Decision Variables (all continuous, ≥ 0)

- **y₀** = dollars invested in Option 1 at t = 0 (matures at t = 2)
- **y₁** = dollars invested in Option 1 at t = 1 (matures at t = 3)
- **z₀** = dollars invested in Option 2 at t = 0 (matures at t = 3)
- **s₀, s₁, s₂** = idle cash held (uninvested) from t = 0→1, t = 1→2, t = 2→3

No borrowing variable is needed: the investor can only allocate **existing** cash, so every constraint is a cash-balance (≤) constraint with nonnegative slack. There is no mechanism (and no need) to take on debt.

## 4. Objective

Maximize total cash at end of year 3 (t = 3):

$$\max\ W_3 = 1.7\,y_1 + 3.0\,z_0 + s_2$$

(Only y₁ and z₀ mature at t = 3; s₂ is cash carried through t = 2→3.)

*Profit-only cross-check:* subtracting the $100k principal, maximizing W₃ is equivalent to maximizing total profit $0.7y_0 + 0.7y_1 + 2.0z_0$ — same optimum, since the coefficients are just the gross returns minus 1 and the principal is fixed.

## 5. Constraints (cash-balance at each point in time)

**t = 0 (start of year 1):**
$$y_0 + z_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**t = 1 (start of year 2):** y₀ matures at ×1.7
$$y_1 + s_1 = 1.7\,y_0 + s_0$$

**t = 2 (start of year 3):** y₁ matures at ×1.7
$$s_2 = 1.7\,y_1 + s_1$$

**t = 3 (end of year 3):** z₀ matures at ×3.0 — this is captured in the objective; no additional constraint is required. (Equivalently, W₃ = 3.0 z₀ + s₂, which is exactly the objective. **No terminal constraint is missing** — the horizon is fully accounted for because every dollar is either matured, idle, or in the objective.)

**Nonnegativity:**
$$y_0,\ y_1,\ z_0,\ s_0,\ s_1,\ s_2 \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. Perfect divisibility of investment amounts (continuous variables).
2. No borrowing; only existing cash can be invested (hence ≤-type balance constraints with idle-cash slack).
3. Idle cash earns 0%.
4. Returns are deterministic and paid at maturity (gross multiples 1.7 and 3.0).
5. Reinvestment of matured proceeds is allowed (y₀ → y₁).
6. Horizon is exactly 3 years; anything maturing after t = 3 is infeasible and thus excluded by variable definition (only y₀, y₁ for Option 1).

## 7. Worked Optimal Solution (sanity check)

Compare the two pure strategies and the natural mixed one.

**Strategy A — Option 1 twice (roll it):**
- t=0: invest 100,000 in y₀ → t=1 proceeds = 170,000
- t=1: invest 170,000 in y₁ → t=2 proceeds = 1.7 × 170,000 = **289,000**
- t=2→3: hold idle → **W₃ = 289,000**

**Strategy B — Option 2 once:**
- t=0: invest 100,000 in z₀ → t=3 proceeds = 3.0 × 100,000 = **300,000**
- **W₃ = 300,000**

**Strategy C — split (check no interior optimum beats both):**
Let x go to Option 1 (rolled) and (100,000 − x) to Option 2.
- Option-1 roll: x → 1.7x at t=1 → 1.7²x = 2.89x at t=2, held to t=3 → 2.89x
- Option 2: 3.0(100,000 − x)
- W₃(x) = 2.89x + 300,000 − 3.0x = 300,000 − 0.11x

This is **decreasing in x**, so the optimum is at x = 0: **all in Option 2.**

**Optimal solution:**

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| y₀ | 0 |
| y₁ | 0 |
| z₀ | 100,000 |
| s₀ | 0 |
| s₁ | 0 |
| s₂ | 0 |
| **W₃** | **300,000** |

**Optimal objective value: $300,000** (profit $200,000).

**Verification of optimality:** Option 2's 3-year gross multiple (3.0) exceeds Option 1 rolled twice (1.7² = 2.89), so Option 2 dominates per dollar over the full horizon. The linear split analysis confirms the corner solution x = 0 is optimal. The LP is therefore solved and verified.

{"description": "Generate a linear (MILP) model for the following investment problem.

An investor has 100,000 yuan to invest at the start of year 1. There are two investment options:
- Option 1: a one-year investment that returns a profit of 0.7 per 1 yuan invested after one year (i.e., 1 yuan becomes 1.7 yuan after one year). Can be reinvested in subsequent years.
- Option 2: a two-year investment that returns a profit of 2 per 1 yuan invested after two years (i.e., 1 yuan becomes 3 yuan after two years). The investment time must be a multiple of two years (money is locked in for a full two-year period).

Goal: maximize the total money available at the end of the third year.

Please formulate as a complete MILP with:
- Decision variables for amounts invested in each option at each year start, and amounts held/idle between periods.
- Cash-balance (flow conservation) constraints for each year start.
- The final objective as total cash at end of year 3.
- Non-negativity constraints.

Assumptions to mark clearly: money not invested earns no interest (idle cash); option 2 funds are tied up for exactly two years and cannot be withdrawn early; option 1 can be repeated each year; all investments are made at the start of a year and returns arrive at the start of the following period(s)."}

messages.content:
# MILP Formulation: Multi-Year Investment Planning

## 1. Problem Setting and Time Convention

We track cash at the **start of each year** (time points $t = 0, 1, 2, 3$), where $t=0$ is the start of year 1 and $t=3$ is the start of year 4 (= end of year 3).

- **Option 1 (1-year):** $x_t$ invested at start of year $t$ returns $1.7\,x_t$ at start of year $t+1$.
- **Option 2 (2-year):** $y_t$ invested at start of year $t$ returns $3\,y_t$ at start of year $t+2$.
- **Idle cash:** $s_t$ held at start of year $t$ (carries to $t+1$ with no interest).

**Key modeling assumption (please verify):** Since the problem says Option 2's "investment time must be a multiple of two years," we interpret this as: any money placed in Option 2 is locked for a full 2-year period, and the *duration of the commitment* must be a multiple of 2 years. Because the horizon is only 3 years, the only feasible 2-year (or 4-year, etc.) windows are those **starting at $t=0$** (matures at $t=2$) and **starting at $t=1$** (matures at $t=3$). A commitment starting at $t=2$ would mature at $t=4$, beyond the horizon, and is therefore not allowed. We model this by restricting $y_t$ to $t \in \{0,1\}$ only.

## 2. Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $x_t$ | Amount invested in Option 1 at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1,2\}$, $x_t \ge 0$ |
| $y_t$ | Amount invested in Option 2 at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1\}$, $y_t \ge 0$ |
| $s_t$ | Idle cash held at start of year $t$ | $t \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, $s_t \ge 0$ |

*(All variables are continuous and non-negative. No binary/integer variables are strictly required here because the "multiple of two years" restriction is enforced structurally by limiting $y_t$ to $t\in\{0,1\}$; see Note in §6.)*

## 3. Objective Function

Maximize total cash at the start of year 4 (end of year 3):

$$\max \; Z = s_3$$

where $s_3$ is the cash balance at $t=3$ after all returns have arrived. (Equivalently, $Z$ = idle cash at $t=3$, since no further investment is possible/needed.)

## 4. Cash-Balance (Flow Conservation) Constraints

**Start of year 1 ($t=0$):** Initial endowment of 100,000 is allocated to Option 1, Option 2, or held idle.

$$x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**Start of year 2 ($t=1$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=0$ + Option 1 return from $t=0$. Allocated to Option 1, Option 2, or held idle.

$$x_1 + y_1 + s_1 = s_0 + 1.7\,x_0$$

**Start of year 3 ($t=2$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=1$ + Option 1 return from $t=1$ + Option 2 return from $t=0$. Allocated to Option 1 or held idle (no new Option 2 allowed, since it would mature after the horizon).

$$x_2 + s_2 = s_1 + 1.7\,x_1 + 3\,y_0$$

**Start of year 4 / end of year 3 ($t=3$):** Incoming cash = idle from $t=2$ + Option 1 return from $t=2$ + Option 2 return from $t=1$. This is terminal wealth.

$$s_3 = s_2 + 1.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_1$$

## 5. Non-Negativity

$$x_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1,2\}, \qquad y_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1\}, \qquad s_t \ge 0 \quad \forall t \in \{0,1,2,3\}$$

## 6. Complete Model (Consolidated)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = s_3 \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_1 + y_1 + s_1 - s_0 - 1.7\,x_0 = 0 \\
& x_2 + s_2 - s_1 - 1.7\,x_1 - 3\,y_0 = 0 \\
& s_3 - s_2 - 1.7\,x_2 - 3\,y_1 = 0 \\
& x_0, x_1, x_2,\; y_0, y_1,\; s_0, s_1, s_2, s_3 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

**Note on integrality:** The phrase "investment time must be a multiple of two years" is enforced here by *structural restriction* (only $y_0, y_1$ exist; $y_2$ is omitted because a 2-year lock starting at $t=2$ matures at $t=4 >$ horizon). If instead the intended meaning were that Option 2 amounts must be integer multiples of some unit (e.g., whole "2-year blocks"), one would add integer variables $n_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with $y_t = U\,n_t$. As stated, no binary variables are needed, so the model is technically an **LP**; the MILP framing is satisfied trivially (zero integer variables). I flag this so you can add integrality if your course requires it.

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Variables:** $x_t$ and $y_t$ capture *how much* goes into each product at each decision epoch; $s_t$ captures *idle cash* (the "slack" that carries over with zero return). The $s_t$ variables are essential to make flow conservation an equality rather than an inequality.
- **Coefficients:** $1.7$ and $3$ are the *gross* returns (principal + profit) per yuan, consistent with "1 yuan becomes 1.7 / 3 yuan." Using gross returns (not profits of 0.7/2) avoids double-counting principal.
- **Timing:** Returns "arrive at the start of the following period(s)," so a $t=0$ Option-1 investment appears on the $t=1$ balance sheet, and a $t=0$ Option-2 investment appears on the $t=2$ balance sheet. This is exactly how the constraints are written.
- **Terminal condition:** $s_3$ is defined by the $t=3$ balance equation, so maximizing $s_3$ maximizes all cash available at end of year 3 (including returns from $x_2$ and $y_1$). No separate "terminal" constraint is needed.
- **Option-2 lock-in:** Enforced by the absence of early-withdrawal terms — $y_0$ only appears at $t=2$, $y_1$ only at $t=3$. There is no way to recover $y_t$ before maturity.
- **No-interest idle cash:** $s_t$ carries to $s_{t+1}$ with coefficient 1 (no growth), as assumed.

## 8. Assumptions Marked Clearly

1. **Idle cash earns no interest** (coefficient 1 in flow constraints).
2. **Option 2 is locked for exactly 2 years**; no early withdrawal, no partial liquidity.
3. **Option 1 is repeatable annually** and fully liquid at each year boundary.
4. **All investments are made at the start of a year**; returns arrive at the start of the maturity year (so they are immediately reinvestable).
5. **"Multiple of two years"** is interpreted as: Option-2 commitments must span a whole 2-year window; within a 3-year horizon only windows starting at $t=0$ and $t=1$ are feasible, hence $y_2$ is excluded.
6. **Continuous, divisible investments** (no minimum lot size); if lot sizes are required, add integer variables as noted in §6.
7. **No taxes, transaction costs, or borrowing** are considered.

# Final Model: Multi-Year Investment Allocation (LP)

## 1. Problem Setting

An investor has **100,000 yuan** at the start of year 1 and may allocate it to two options. Uninvested cash is held at 0% interest. The goal is to **maximize total cash at the end of year 3** (start of year 4).

| Option | Lock-up | Gross return per 1 yuan | Profit per 1 yuan |
|--------|---------|--------------------------|--------------------|
| 1 | 1 year (repeatable) | 1.7 | 0.7 |
| 2 | 2 years (multiple of 2) | 3.0 | 2.0 |

**Structural note:** Option 2 must be committed for a full 2-year window. Within a 3-year horizon, only windows starting at t=0 (matures t=2) and t=1 (matures t=3) are feasible; a start at t=2 would mature at t=4, beyond the horizon. This is enforced **structurally by defining only y₀ and y₁**, so **no integer variables are needed** — the model is a pure LP.

## 2. Time-Indexing

| Index | Meaning | Cash events |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| t = 0 | Start of year 1 | 100,000 available; start Option 1 (x₀) or Option 2 (y₀) |
| t = 1 | Start of year 2 | x₀ matures (×1.7); start Option 1 (x₁) or Option 2 (y₁) |
| t = 2 | Start of year 3 | x₁ matures (×1.7); y₀ matures (×3.0); start Option 1 (x₂) |
| t = 3 | Start of year 4 = **end of year 3** | x₂ matures (×1.7); y₁ matures (×3.0); objective measured here |

## 3. Decision Variables (all continuous, ≥ 0)

- **x₀, x₁, x₂** = amount invested in Option 1 at start of years 1, 2, 3
- **y₀, y₁** = amount invested in Option 2 at start of years 1, 2 (mature at t=2, t=3)
- **s₀, s₁, s₂, s₃** = idle cash carried from t→t+1

No borrowing variable is needed: the investor can only allocate existing cash, so each balance is an equality with nonnegative idle-cash slack.

## 4. Objective

$$\max \; Z = s_3$$

where s₃ is total cash at end of year 3 (after all returns arrive).

*Cross-check:* Since the 100,000 principal is fixed, maximizing s₃ is equivalent to maximizing total profit 0.7(x₀+x₁+x₂) + 2(y₀+y₁) — same optimum.

## 5. Constraints (cash balance at each time point)

**t = 0 (start of year 1):**
$$x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**t = 1 (start of year 2):** x₀ matures ×1.7
$$x_1 + y_1 + s_1 = s_0 + 1.7\,x_0$$

**t = 2 (start of year 3):** x₁ matures ×1.7, y₀ matures ×3.0; no new Option 2 (would mature past horizon)
$$x_2 + s_2 = s_1 + 1.7\,x_1 + 3\,y_0$$

**t = 3 (end of year 3):** x₂ matures ×1.7, y₁ matures ×3.0; terminal wealth
$$s_3 = s_2 + 1.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_1$$

**Nonnegativity:**
$$x_0,x_1,x_2,\; y_0,y_1,\; s_0,s_1,s_2,s_3 \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. Perfect divisibility of investment amounts (continuous).
2. No borrowing — only existing cash can be invested.
3. Idle cash earns 0%.
4. Deterministic gross returns of 1.7 (Option 1) and 3.0 (Option 2) paid at maturity.
5. Matured proceeds are immediately reinvestable.
6. Horizon is exactly 3 years; Option 2 commitments starting at t=2 are infeasible (mature at t=4) and excluded.
7. No taxes, transaction costs, or minimum lot sizes.

## 7. Worked Optimal Solution

**Strategy A — Option 1 rolled each year:**
100,000 → ×1.7 → 170,000 → ×1.7 → 289,000 → ×1.7 → **491,300**

**Strategy B — Option 2 once:**
100,000 → ×3.0 → **300,000**

**Mixed check:** Let x go to Option 1 (rolled all 3 years) and (100,000 − x) to Option 2:
- Option 1 path: 1.7³·x = 4.913x
- Option 2 path: 3.0·(100,000 − x)
- Z(x) = 4.913x + 300,000 − 3.0x = 300,000 + 1.913x → **increasing in x**

So the optimum is at x = 100,000: **all in Option 1, rolled each year.**

**Optimal solution:**

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| x₀ | 100,000 |
| x₁ | 170,000 |
| x₂ | 289,000 |
| y₀ | 0 |
| y₁ | 0 |
| s₀, s₁, s₂ | 0 |
| s₃ | 491,300 |
| **Z** | **491,300** |

**Optimal objective value: 491,300 yuan** (profit 391,300 yuan).

**Verification:** Option 1's three-year gross multiple (1.7³ = 4.913) exceeds Option 2's (3.0), so Option 1 dominates per yuan over the full horizon; the linear split analysis confirms the corner solution x = 100,000 is optimal.

# Final Model: Multi-Year Investment Allocation (LP)

## 1. Problem Setting

An investor has **100,000 yuan** at the start of year 1 and may allocate it to two options. Uninvested cash is held at 0% interest. The goal is to **maximize total cash at the end of year 3** (start of year 4).

| Option | Lock-up | Gross return per 1 yuan | Profit per 1 yuan |
|--------|---------|--------------------------|--------------------|
| 1 | 1 year (repeatable) | 1.7 | 0.7 |
| 2 | 2 years (multiple of 2) | 3.0 | 2.0 |

**Structural note:** Option 2 must be committed for a full 2-year window. Within a 3-year horizon, only windows starting at t=0 (matures t=2) and t=1 (matures t=3) are feasible; a start at t=2 would mature at t=4, beyond the horizon. This is enforced **structurally by defining only y₀ and y₁**, so **no integer variables are needed** — the model is a pure LP.

## 2. Time-Indexing

| Index | Meaning | Cash events |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| t = 0 | Start of year 1 | 100,000 available; start Option 1 (x₀) or Option 2 (y₀) |
| t = 1 | Start of year 2 | x₀ matures (×1.7); start Option 1 (x₁) or Option 2 (y₁) |
| t = 2 | Start of year 3 | x₁ matures (×1.7); y₀ matures (×3.0); start Option 1 (x₂) |
| t = 3 | Start of year 4 = **end of year 3** | x₂ matures (×1.7); y₁ matures (×3.0); objective measured here |

## 3. Decision Variables (all continuous, ≥ 0)

- **x₀, x₁, x₂** = amount invested in Option 1 at start of years 1, 2, 3
- **y₀, y₁** = amount invested in Option 2 at start of years 1, 2 (mature at t=2, t=3)
- **s₀, s₁, s₂, s₃** = idle cash carried from t→t+1

No borrowing variable is needed: the investor can only allocate existing cash, so each balance is an equality with nonnegative idle-cash slack.

## 4. Objective

$$\max \; Z = s_3$$

where s₃ is total cash at end of year 3 (after all returns arrive).

*Cross-check:* Since the 100,000 principal is fixed, maximizing s₃ is equivalent to maximizing total profit 0.7(x₀+x₁+x₂) + 2(y₀+y₁) — same optimum.

## 5. Constraints (cash balance at each time point)

**t = 0 (start of year 1):**
$$x_0 + y_0 + s_0 = 100{,}000$$

**t = 1 (start of year 2):** x₀ matures ×1.7
$$x_1 + y_1 + s_1 = s_0 + 1.7\,x_0$$

**t = 2 (start of year 3):** x₁ matures ×1.7, y₀ matures ×3.0; no new Option 2 (would mature past horizon)
$$x_2 + s_2 = s_1 + 1.7\,x_1 + 3\,y_0$$

**t = 3 (end of year 3):** x₂ matures ×1.7, y₁ matures ×3.0; terminal wealth
$$s_3 = s_2 + 1.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_1$$

**Nonnegativity:**
$$x_0,x_1,x_2,\; y_0,y_1,\; s_0,s_1,s_2,s_3 \ge 0$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. Perfect divisibility of investment amounts (continuous).
2. No borrowing — only existing cash can be invested.
3. Idle cash earns 0%.
4. Deterministic gross returns of 1.7 (Option 1) and 3.0 (Option 2) paid at maturity.
5. Matured proceeds are immediately reinvestable.
6. Horizon is exactly 3 years; Option 2 commitments starting at t=2 are infeasible (mature at t=4) and excluded.
7. No taxes, transaction costs, or minimum lot sizes.

## 7. Worked Optimal Solution

**Strategy A — Option 1 rolled each year:**
100,000 → ×1.7 → 170,000 → ×1.7 → 289,000 → ×1.7 → **491,300**

**Strategy B — Option 2 once:**
100,000 → ×3.0 → **300,000**

**Mixed check:** Let x go to Option 1 (rolled all 3 years) and (100,000 − x) to Option 2:
- Option 1 path: 1.7³·x = 4.913x
- Option 2 path: 3.0·(100,000 − x)
- Z(x) = 4.913x + 300,000 − 3.0x = 300,000 + 1.913x → **increasing in x**

So the optimum is at x = 100,000: **all in Option 1, rolled each year.**

**Optimal solution:**

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| x₀ | 100,000 |
| x₁ | 170,000 |
| x₂ | 289,000 |
| y₀ | 0 |
| y₁ | 0 |
| s₀, s₁, s₂ | 0 |
| s₃ | 491,300 |
| **Z** | **491,300** |

**Optimal objective value: 491,300 yuan** (profit 391,300 yuan).

**Verification:** Option 1's three-year gross multiple (1.7³ = 4.913) exceeds Option 2's (3.0), so Option 1 dominates per yuan over the full horizon; the linear split analysis confirms the corner solution x = 100,000 is optimal.

Model 1:
# MILP: Multi-Period Investment Planning

## Problem Summary

An investor has **100,000 yuan** at the start of year 1 and must plan investments over a **3-year horizon** using two options:

- **Option 1 (1-year):** Each yuan returns **1.7 yuan** after one year. Available at the start of years 1, 2, and 3.
- **Option 2 (2-year):** Each yuan returns **3.0 yuan** after two years (locked for exactly 2 years). Available at the start of years 1 and 2 only.
- **Cash:** Idle money can be carried forward with no interest.

**Objective:** Maximize total cash at the end of year 3.

---

## Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_{1,1} \ge 0$ | Amount invested in Option 1 at start of year 1 |
| $x_{1,2} \ge 0$ | Amount invested in Option 1 at start of year 2 |
| $x_{1,3} \ge 0$ | Amount invested in Option 1 at start of year 3 |
| $x_{2,1} \ge 0$ | Amount invested in Option 2 at start of year 1 (matures end of year 2) |
| $x_{2,2} \ge 0$ | Amount invested in Option 2 at start of year 2 (matures end of year 3) |
| $c_0 \ge 0$ | Cash held at start of year 1 (before any investment) |
| $c_1 \ge 0$ | Cash carried from start of year 1 to start of year 2 |
| $c_2 \ge 0$ | Cash carried from start of year 2 to start of year 3 |
| $c_3 \ge 0$ | Cash at end of year 3 (terminal wealth) |

All variables are **continuous and non-negative**. (The model is linear; if integer investment units were required, integrality could be imposed on the $x$ variables — but here fractional yuan are allowed, so it is an LP. The MILP framework below is stated generally.)

---

## Objective Function

Maximize terminal cash at the end of year 3:

$$\max \; Z = c_3$$

---

## Constraints

### (1) Initial cash endowment (start of year 1)

Total cash available equals investments placed plus cash carried forward:

$$c_0 = 100{,}000$$

$$x_{1,1} + x_{2,1} + c_1 = c_0$$

### (2) Cash balance at start of year 2

Inflows: cash carried from year 1 ($c_1$) plus Option 1 maturing from year 1 ($1.7\,x_{1,1}$).
Outflows: new investments plus cash carried to year 3.

$$x_{1,2} + x_{2,2} + c_2 = c_1 + 1.7\,x_{1,1}$$

### (3) Cash balance at start of year 3

Inflows: cash carried from year 2 ($c_2$), Option 1 maturing from year 2 ($1.7\,x_{1,2}$), and Option 2 maturing from year 1 ($3.0\,x_{2,1}$).
Outflows: Option 1 investment in year 3 plus terminal cash.

$$x_{1,3} + c_3 = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1}$$

### (4) Terminal cash definition (end of year 3)

At the end of year 3, all remaining investments mature: Option 1 placed in year 3 returns $1.7\,x_{1,3}$; Option 2 placed in year 2 returns $3.0\,x_{2,2}$. Terminal cash is whatever was carried plus these maturities:

$$c_3 = c_3^{\text{(from balance)}} + 1.7\,x_{1,3} + 3.0\,x_{2,2}$$

To keep the model clean, fold this into the year-3 balance by treating $c_3$ as *post-maturity* terminal wealth. Rewrite constraint (3) as:

$$c_3 = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1} + 1.7\,x_{1,3} + 3.0\,x_{2,2}$$

and drop the separate $x_{1,3}$ outflow term (since year-3 Option 1 investment matures within the horizon and contributes to terminal wealth). Equivalently, keep (3) as written and add the terminal maturity equation. **The consolidated form is:**

$$\boxed{c_3 = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1} + 1.7\,x_{1,3} + 3.0\,x_{2,2}}$$

with the year-3 balance written as:

$$x_{1,3} + c_3^{\text{pre}} = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1}$$

### (5) Non-negativity

$$x_{1,1}, x_{1,2}, x_{1,3}, x_{2,1}, x_{2,2}, c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3 \ge 0$$

---

## Compact Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = c_3 \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_{1,1} + x_{2,1} + c_1 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_{1,2} + x_{2,2} + c_2 = c_1 + 1.7\,x_{1,1} \\
& c_3 = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1} + 1.7\,x_{1,3} + 3.0\,x_{2,2} \\
& x_{1,3} \le c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1} \quad \text{(year-3 funding feasibility)} \\
& x_{i,t} \ge 0,\; c_k \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Explanation of Model Elements

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| **$x_{1,t}$** | Amounts in the 1-year option; each generates a 1.7× return one period later. |
| **$x_{2,t}$** | Amounts in the 2-year option; each generates a 3.0× return two periods later. Only $t=1,2$ are feasible (a year-3 start would mature after the horizon). |
| **$c_k$** | Cash balances linking periods; they enforce that money is conserved — every yuan is either invested or held. |
| **Balance constraints** | Enforce **cash-flow conservation** at each decision epoch: available cash = new investments + cash carried forward. |
| **Return coefficients (1.7, 3.0)** | Encode the profit rates (0.7 and 2.0 per yuan) as gross multipliers. |
| **Objective $c_3$** | Terminal wealth at end of year 3, including all maturities. |
| **Linear structure** | All constraints are linear equalities/inequalities; the model is an LP. If investments must be in whole-yuan or discrete bundles, add $x_{i,t}\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ to obtain a genuine MILP. |

**Optimal intuition:** Because Option 2 yields a 3.0× return over 2 years (≈73% annualized) versus 1.7× per year (70%), the two-year option is slightly better per year, so the optimal policy tends to route as much as possible into $x_{2,1}$ and then $x_{2,2}$, subject to liquidity timing — the model will determine the exact allocation.

Model 2:
# MILP: Multi-Period Investment Planning

## 1. Problem Restatement

An investor has **100,000 yuan** at the start of year 1 and plans over a **3-year horizon**. Two investment products and a cash account are available. The goal is to **maximize cash at the end of year 3**.

---

## 2. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $t \in \{1,2,3\}$ | Start of year $t$ (decision epochs) |
| $t=4$ | End of year 3 (terminal point, no decisions) |

Two investment types:
- **Type A** (1-year): available at start of years 1, 2, 3.
- **Type B** (2-year): available at start of years 1, 2 only (must mature by end of year 3).

---

## 3. Parameters

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $W_0$ | 100,000 | Initial cash (yuan) |
| $r_A$ | 1.7 | Multiplier for Type A after 1 year (principal + 0.7 profit) |
| $r_B$ | 3.0 | Multiplier for Type B after 2 years (principal + 2 profit) |

---

## 4. Decision Variables

All variables are **continuous and non-negative** (amounts in yuan):

| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{A,t}$ | $t=1,2,3$ | Amount invested in Type A at start of year $t$ |
| $x_{B,t}$ | $t=1,2$ | Amount invested in Type B at start of year $t$ |
| $c_t$ | $t=1,2,3$ | Cash carried forward from start of year $t$ to start of year $t+1$ (i.e., held idle during year $t$) |

> **Note on integrality:** The problem statement says "All linear" and describes continuous money amounts. No binary or integer variables are required — this is a pure **LP**. If a minimum investment lot size were imposed, binaries would be needed; none is given, so the model is linear continuous. (I note this explicitly since the request says "MILP"; the formulation below is the correct linear model, and I flag where integrality *could* be added.)

---

## 5. Objective Function

Maximize terminal cash at the end of year 3. Terminal cash consists of:
- Cash carried out of year 3: $c_3$
- Maturity of Type A started in year 3: $r_A\, x_{A,3}$
- Maturity of Type B started in year 2: $r_B\, x_{B,2}$

$$\boxed{\max\; Z = c_3 + r_A\, x_{A,3} + r_B\, x_{B,2}}$$

(Type B started in year 1 matures at end of year 2 and is *reinvested* within the horizon, so it does not appear directly in the terminal expression — it appears through the year-3 balance constraint.)

---

## 6. Constraints

### 6.1 Cash-flow balance at start of year 1
All initial cash is either invested or carried forward:
$$x_{A,1} + x_{B,1} + c_1 = W_0$$

### 6.2 Cash-flow balance at start of year 2
Available cash = cash carried from year 1 **plus** maturity of Type A started in year 1:
$$x_{A,2} + x_{B,2} + c_2 = c_1 + r_A\, x_{A,1}$$

### 6.3 Cash-flow balance at start of year 3
Available cash = cash carried from year 2 **plus** maturity of Type A started in year 2 **plus** maturity of Type B started in year 1:
$$x_{A,3} + c_3 = c_2 + r_A\, x_{A,2} + r_B\, x_{B,1}$$

> There is no $x_{B,3}$ because a 2-year product started in year 3 would mature after the horizon (end of year 5), which is infeasible. This is why Type B is only indexed $t=1,2$.

### 6.4 Non-negativity
$$x_{A,1}, x_{A,2}, x_{A,3},\; x_{B,1}, x_{B,2},\; c_1, c_2, c_3 \;\ge\; 0$$

---

## 7. Complete Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\quad & Z = c_3 + 1.7\,x_{A,3} + 3.0\,x_{B,2} \\
\text{s.t.}\quad
& x_{A,1} + x_{B,1} + c_1 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_{A,2} + x_{B,2} + c_2 = c_1 + 1.7\,x_{A,1} \\
& x_{A,3} + c_3 = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{A,2} + 3.0\,x_{B,1} \\
& x_{A,t} \ge 0 \quad t=1,2,3 \\
& x_{B,t} \ge 0 \quad t=1,2 \\
& c_t \ge 0 \quad t=1,2,3
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 8. Explanation of Model Elements

**Why these variables.** Each investment decision is tied to a *start time*, because the same product can be entered in different years and the cash-flow timing differs. Cash carried forward $c_t$ is needed because money may sit idle (zero interest) between investments — the balance constraints would otherwise force all cash to be invested every period, which is not required.

**Why the balance constraints take this form.** At the start of each year, the only sources of funds are (i) cash carried in from the prior year and (ii) maturities of investments that come due exactly then. The only uses are new investments and cash carried out. Setting sources = uses gives one equality per decision epoch. This is the standard **cash-flow (source–use) formulation** for multi-period financial planning.

**Timing / maturity logic.**
- Type A entered at $t$ returns $1.7x$ at $t+1$ → appears as a *source* in the balance of year $t+1$.
- Type B entered at $t$ returns $3.0x$ at $t+2$ → appears as a *source* in the balance of year $t+2$ (year 2 for $t=1$, year 3 for $t=2$).
- Type B entered in year 1 matures at end of year 2, so its proceeds fund year-3 decisions (captured in constraint 6.3).

**Why the objective is written that way.** At the end of year 3, wealth equals idle cash $c_3$ plus whatever matures at that instant: Type A from year 3 and Type B from year 2. Everything else has already been recycled into these or into $c_3$ through the balance constraints, so this expression correctly equals total terminal wealth.

**Linearity.** Every constraint and the objective are linear in the decision variables; the multipliers $1.7$ and $3.0$ are constants. Hence the model is a linear program. If the problem required **indivisible** investments (e.g., minimum lot sizes, or "invest or don't"), one would add binary indicators $y_{A,t}, y_{B,t}$ with big-M linking constraints $x \le M\,y$ and $x \ge m\,y$, converting it to a genuine MILP — but no such requirement is stated, so the continuous LP above is the faithful model.

**Solvability.** With 8 variables and 3 equality constraints, the LP is small and can be solved by inspection or any LP solver. (For reference, the optimal policy invests the full 100,000 in Type B in year 1, since $3.0$ over two years dominates rolling two 1-year investments at $1.7^2 = 2.89$; the model will confirm this automatically.)

# MILP Formulation: Multi-Period Investment Planning

## Problem Summary

An investor has **100,000 yuan** to allocate over a **3-year horizon** among:
- **Option 1 (1-year investment):** Each yuan returns **1.7 yuan** after one year. Available to start at the beginning of years 1, 2, and 3.
- **Option 2 (2-year investment):** Each yuan returns **3.0 yuan** after two years (must be held exactly two years). Available to start at the beginning of year 1 (matures end of year 2) or year 2 (matures end of year 3).
- **Cash:** Can be carried forward with no interest.

**Objective:** Maximize total cash at the end of year 3.

---

## Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| $x_{1,t} \ge 0$ | Amount (yuan) invested in **Option 1** at the **start of year $t$**, for $t \in \{1,2,3\}$ |
| $x_{2,t} \ge 0$ | Amount (yuan) invested in **Option 2** at the **start of year $t$**, for $t \in \{1,2\}$ |
| $c_t \ge 0$ | Cash carried forward **from the start of year $t$ to the start of year $t+1$**, for $t \in \{1,2,3\}$ (with $c_3$ = cash held at end of year 3) |

All variables are **continuous and non-negative**. (No integer/binary variables are required — the problem is a pure LP; see note below.)

---

## Objective Function

Maximize total cash at the end of year 3. Cash at the end of year 3 consists of:
- Cash carried forward from year 3: $c_3$
- Maturity of Option 1 started in year 3: $1.7\,x_{1,3}$
- Maturity of Option 2 started in year 2: $3.0\,x_{2,2}$

$$\boxed{\max \; Z = c_3 + 1.7\,x_{1,3} + 3.0\,x_{2,2}}$$

> *Note:* Option 2 started in year 1 matures at the end of year 2 and is reinvested through the year-2 balance constraint; Option 1 started in years 1–2 likewise rolls through the balance constraints. Only the terminal inflows appear directly in the objective.

---

## Constraints

### Cash-flow balance at the start of each year

**Start of Year 1** — initial endowment of 100,000 yuan:
$$x_{1,1} + x_{2,1} + c_1 = 100{,}000$$

**Start of Year 2** — available cash = carried cash $c_1$ + maturity of Option 1 from year 1 ($1.7\,x_{1,1}$):
$$x_{1,2} + x_{2,2} + c_2 = c_1 + 1.7\,x_{1,1}$$

**Start of Year 3** — available cash = carried cash $c_2$ + maturity of Option 1 from year 2 ($1.7\,x_{1,2}$) + maturity of Option 2 from year 1 ($3.0\,x_{2,1}$):
$$x_{1,3} + c_3 = c_2 + 1.7\,x_{1,2} + 3.0\,x_{2,1}$$

### Non-negativity
$$x_{1,1},\,x_{1,2},\,x_{1,3},\,x_{2,1},\,x_{2,2},\,c_1,\,c_2,\,c_3 \ge 0$$

---

## Complete Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = c_3 + 1.7\,x_{1,3} + 3.0\,x_{2,2} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_{1,1} + x_{2,1} + c_1 = 100{,}000 \\
& x_{1,2} + x_{2,2} + c_2 - c_1 - 1.7\,x_{1,1} = 0 \\
& x_{1,3} + c_3 - c_2 - 1.7\,x_{1,2} - 3.0\,x_{2,1} = 0 \\
& x_{1,1}, x_{1,2}, x_{1,3}, x_{2,1}, x_{2,2}, c_1, c_2, c_3 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Explanation of Model Elements

**Decision variables.**
- $x_{1,t}$ captures the 1-year instrument, which can be *rolled over* each year — hence three separate variables (one per start year). The same money can appear in multiple $x_{1,\cdot}$ variables across years, linked by the balance constraints.
- $x_{2,t}$ captures the 2-year instrument, which can only start in years 1 or 2 (a year-3 start would mature after the horizon, so it is excluded).
- $c_t$ represents idle cash. It earns no interest but preserves liquidity, so it acts as the "slack" that makes each balance equation feasible.

**Objective.** Only cash flows *received by the end of year 3* count. These are the year-3 rollover of Option 1, the year-2 start of Option 2, and any residual cash $c_3$. Earlier maturities are automatically captured because they are *reinvested* through the balance constraints (e.g., Option 2 started in year 1 appears as $3.0\,x_{2,1}$ on the right-hand side of the year-3 balance).

**Balance constraints.** Each states that *all cash available at the start of a year is fully accounted for*: it is either invested (in either option) or carried forward. Because the constraints are equalities and all variables are non-negative, no cash is created or destroyed — this enforces consistent cash-flow accounting.

**Linearity.** Returns are proportional to investment (1.7× and 3.0×), and all constraints are linear equalities. The model is therefore a **linear program**; the "MILP" framing holds trivially with no integrality restrictions needed (amounts are continuous yuan). If integer-yuan or minimum-investment/lot-size rules were added, binary or integer variables would be introduced, but none are required here.

**Why this is optimal to solve as an LP.** With continuous variables and a single linear objective, the optimal solution will be a vertex — typically investing fully in whichever instrument gives the highest effective annual return. Option 1 yields 70% per year; Option 2 yields $\sqrt{3}-1 \approx 73.2\%$ per year, so Option 2 is slightly better per year but locks up capital for two years, creating a genuine trade-off the LP resolves exactly.
