# MILP: Nurse Shift Scheduling

## 1. Sets and Indices

- **Periods** $p \in P = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, each 4 hours long:
  - P1: 02:00–06:00, demand 10
  - P2: 06:00–10:00, demand 15
  - P3: 10:00–14:00, demand 25
  - P4: 14:00–18:00, demand 20
  - P5: 18:00–22:00, demand 18
  - P6: 22:00–02:00, demand 12
- **Shift batches** $i \in I = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, starting at 02:00, 06:00, 10:00, 14:00, 18:00, 22:00 respectively. Each shift covers **two consecutive periods**.

## 2. Parameters

| Parameter | Value | Description |
|---|---|---|
| $d_p$ | (10, 15, 25, 20, 18, 12) | Demand (nurses) in period $p$ |
| $c^R$ | 80 | Cost per regular 8h shift |
| $c^C$ | 120 | Cost per contract 8h shift |
| $a_{pi}$ | 0/1 | Coverage matrix: 1 if shift starting in batch $i$ covers period $p$ |

**Coverage matrix** $a_{pi}$ (shift $i$ covers periods $i$ and $i+1$, with wrap-around $6+1=1$):

| Period \ Start | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 (2–6) | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| P2 (6–10) | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| P3 (10–14) | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| P4 (14–18) | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| P5 (18–22) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| P6 (22–2) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |

## 3. Decision Variables

- $x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: number of **regular** nurses starting in batch $i$ (8h shift).
- $y_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: number of **contract** nurses starting in batch $i$ (8h shift).
- $z \in \{0, 1\}$: binary indicator — $z = 1$ if **any** contract nurse is hired, $z = 0$ otherwise.

## 4. Objective Function

Minimize total cost:

$$\min \; 80 \sum_{i=1}^{6} x_i \;+\; 120 \sum_{i=1}^{6} y_i$$

## 5. Constraints

**(a) Coverage constraints** — for each period, nurses from the two shifts covering it must meet demand:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_6 + y_1 + y_6 &\ge 10 && \text{(P1)}\\
x_1 + x_2 + y_1 + y_2 &\ge 15 && \text{(P2)}\\
x_2 + x_3 + y_2 + y_3 &\ge 25 && \text{(P3)}\\
x_3 + x_4 + y_3 + y_4 &\ge 20 && \text{(P4)}\\
x_4 + x_5 + y_4 + y_5 &\ge 18 && \text{(P5)}\\
x_5 + x_6 + y_5 + y_6 &\ge 12 && \text{(P6)}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(b) Contract-hiring indicator** — link $z$ to contract usage (big-$M$ formulation). Let $M$ be a safe upper bound on total contract nurses (e.g., $M = \sum_p d_p = 100$):

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{6} y_i \le M \cdot z
$$

This forces $z = 1$ whenever any contract nurse is hired, and allows $z = 0$ only if $\sum_i y_i = 0$. (The solver will keep $z=0$ unless contract nurses are actually needed, since contract nurses are more expensive.)

**(c) Variable domains:**

$$
x_i, y_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \qquad z \in \{0, 1\}
$$

## 6. Model Elements Explained

- **Shift structure:** Each nurse works a continuous 8h block = exactly 2 consecutive 4h periods. Because batch starts are spaced 4h apart, the coverage matrix is a "circular band" — each period is covered by exactly two batches (its own start and the previous start).
- **Regular vs. contract:** Both types have identical coverage; they differ only in cost (\$80 vs. \$120). The MILP will use regular nurses first because they are cheaper; contract nurses appear only when regular capacity (limited by the 2-period shift structure) cannot meet demand.
- **Integer variables:** Nurse counts must be whole numbers — hence integer (not continuous) variables.
- **Binary $z$:** Answers the "whether to hire contract nurses" question. It is 1 iff any contract nurse is used. The big-$M$ constraint is the standard linearization of the logical implication "$\sum y_i > 0 \Rightarrow z = 1$."
- **Feasibility note:** P3 (demand 25) can only be covered by batches 2 and 3, so $x_2 + x_3 + y_2 + y_3 \ge 25$ is the binding bottleneck; this is where contract nurses are most likely needed.

Model 2:
# MILP: Nurse Shift Scheduling

## 1. Sets and Indices

Let $i \in \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ index the six 4-hour periods of the day and the six corresponding shift-start batches (batch $i$ starts at the beginning of period $i$).

| Period | Time | Demand |
|--------|------|--------|
| P1 | 02:00–06:00 | 10 |
| P2 | 06:00–10:00 | 15 |
| P3 | 10:00–14:00 | 25 |
| P4 | 14:00–18:00 | 20 |
| P5 | 18:00–22:00 | 18 |
| P6 | 22:00–02:00 | 12 |

## 2. Decision Variables

- $x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: number of **regular** nurses starting batch $i$ (work 8 h = periods $i$ and $i+1$).
- $y_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: number of **contract** nurses starting batch $i$ (work 8 h = periods $i$ and $i+1$).

(Period indices wrap: period $7 \equiv 1$.)

## 3. Objective Function

Minimize total daily cost (regular \$80/shift, contract \$120/shift):

$$\min \; Z = 80\sum_{i=1}^{6} x_i + 120\sum_{i=1}^{6} y_i$$

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Coverage constraints
Each period $j$ is covered by nurses who started in period $j$ (first half of shift) and those who started in period $j-1$ (second half of shift). With period indices mod 6:

$$
(x_j + x_{j-1}) + (y_j + y_{j-1}) \ge d_j, \qquad j = 1,\dots,6
$$

where $x_0 \equiv x_6$, $y_0 \equiv y_6$. Explicitly:

- P1: $x_1 + x_6 + y_1 + y_6 \ge 10$
- P2: $x_2 + x_1 + y_2 + y_1 \ge 15$
- P3: $x_3 + x_2 + y_3 + y_2 \ge 25$
- P4: $x_4 + x_3 + y_4 + y_3 \ge 20$
- P5: $x_5 + x_4 + y_5 + y_4 \ge 18$
- P6: $x_6 + x_5 + y_6 + y_5 \ge 12$

### 4.2 Integrality and non-negativity

$$x_i, y_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \qquad i = 1,\dots,6$$

## 5. Contract-Nurse Decision (Whether to Hire)

Introduce a binary indicator $z \in \{0,1\}$: $z = 1$ means contract nurses are used.

**Linking (big-M) constraints.** Let $M$ be a valid upper bound on total contract nurses (e.g. $M = \sum_j d_j = 100$, since no more than total demand is ever needed):

$$y_i \le M\, z, \qquad i = 1,\dots,6$$

These force $y_i = 0$ for all $i$ when $z = 0$. The solver will set $z = 1$ only if regular nurses alone cannot satisfy coverage (because contract nurses are strictly more expensive, $120 > 80$ per shift, the optimizer avoids them whenever feasible).

**Optional explicit "prefer regular" objective term** (to break ties and make the preference explicit):

$$\min \; Z = 80\sum_i x_i + 120\sum_i y_i + \varepsilon\, z, \qquad \varepsilon > 0 \text{ small}$$

Since any use of a contract nurse adds $\ge 120$, a small $\varepsilon$ (e.g. $\varepsilon = 1$) only breaks ties in favor of $z=0$ and never changes the true cost optimum.

## 6. Complete Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & 80\sum_{i=1}^{6} x_i + 120\sum_{i=1}^{6} y_i + \varepsilon z \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_j + x_{j-1} + y_j + y_{j-1} \ge d_j, && j=1,\dots,6 \\
& y_i \le M z, && i=1,\dots,6 \\
& x_i, y_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, && i=1,\dots,6 \\
& z \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$
with $d = (10,15,25,20,18,12)$, indices mod 6, $M = 100$, $\varepsilon = 1$.

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Shift structure / coverage matrix.** Each 8-hour shift spans exactly two consecutive 4-hour periods, so period $j$ is staffed by batch $j$ (first half) and batch $j-1$ (second half). The wrap-around ($x_0 = x_6$) captures the overnight P6→P1 link. This "two consecutive periods" structure is what makes the coverage constraints two-term sums rather than arbitrary combinations.
- **Variables.** $x_i, y_i$ are integer headcounts per batch — nurses are indivisible, so integrality is required (this is what makes it an MILP rather than an LP).
- **Objective.** Linear in headcounts; regular nurses are cheaper per shift (\$80 vs \$120), so the optimizer naturally maximizes regular usage first.
- **Coverage constraints.** Lower bounds only (over-staffing is allowed but costly, so the optimum will be tight where possible). Demands are period-specific, capturing the peak at P3 (25) and trough at P1 (10).
- **Contract decision ($z$ + big-M).** The binary $z$ and linking constraints encode the logical "hire contract nurses only if needed." Because contract nurses are strictly more expensive, the cost-minimizing solution already avoids them when regular staffing suffices; $z$ makes this an explicit, auditable decision and the $\varepsilon z$ term removes any ambiguity in ties.
- **Why contract nurses may be needed.** With only 8-hour shifts starting at fixed 4-hour boundaries, the regular workforce may be unable to meet a peaked demand profile (e.g., P3 = 25) without over-staffing other periods; contract nurses add flexibility at higher cost. The MILP determines the cheapest mix.

| P2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| P3 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| P4 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

- **P6 (22–02):** $x_5 + x_6 + y_5 + y_6 \geq 12$

### 5.3 Integrality and non-negativity

$$x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, \quad y_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \quad \forall i \in I$$
$$z \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Shift structure:** Because each nurse works exactly two consecutive 4-hour periods, each period is covered by exactly two shift batches. This is what makes the coverage constraints simple two-variable sums (with wraparound for P1 and P6).
- **Two nurse types:** Regular ($80/shift) and contract ($120/shift) nurses are modeled as separate integer variables per start batch, so the model can choose the cheapest mix at each batch.
- **Cost minimization:** The objective weights regular shifts at \$80 and contract shifts at \$120, so the solver naturally prefers regular nurses and uses contract nurses only when the shift structure prevents meeting demand with regular staff alone.
- **Binary $z$ and big-$M$:** The indicator variable $z$ answers the "should we hire contract nurses at all?" question. The constraint $\sum y_i \le M z$ links the binary to the contract-hiring decision. Because $z$ does not appear in the objective, the solver is free to set $z=0$ whenever $\sum y_i = 0$; the model is therefore consistent with the policy "hire contract nurses only if regular alone cannot meet demand." (If a strict decision output is desired, one can add a tiny penalty $\varepsilon z$ to the objective or simply report $z$ from the optimal solution.)
- **Integrality:** Nurses are indivisible, so $x_i, y_i$ are integer variables — making this a genuine MILP rather than a pure LP.
- **Feasibility note:** Because the model allows $y_i$ to be arbitrarily large, the problem is always feasible; the interesting question the model answers is the *minimum-cost* staffing plan and whether $z=0$ (regular-only) is achievable.

# Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Model: Pollution-Minimizing Transportation Mode Selection

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $i \in \mathcal{I} = \{C, T, B\}$: transportation modes, where $C$ = car, $T$ = truck, $B$ = bus.

## 2. Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Value |
|---|---|---|
| $p_i$ | Pollution per trip of mode $i$ | $p_C = 100$, $p_T = 80$, $p_B = 110$ |
| $c_i$ | Capacity (product units) per trip of mode $i$ | $c_C = 25$, $c_T = 30$, $c_B = 40$ |
| $D$ | Minimum total demand to be transported | $500$ |
| $\bar{x}_T$ | Maximum number of truck trips | $10$ |
| $\bar{N}$ | Maximum total number of trips | $15$ |
| $M$ | Big-M constant (upper bound on any trip count) | $M = 15$ |
| $K$ | Maximum number of modes that may be used | $2$ |

## 3. Decision Variables

- $x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: number of trips using mode $i$, for $i \in \{C, T, B\}$.
- $y_i \in \{0,1\}$: binary indicator equal to 1 if mode $i$ is used (i.e., $x_i \ge 1$), 0 otherwise.

## 4. Objective Function

Minimize total pollution:

$$\min \; Z = 100\,x_C + 80\,x_T + 110\,x_B$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Demand satisfaction** — at least 500 units must be transported:

$$25\,x_C + 30\,x_T + 40\,x_B \ge 500$$

**(C2) Truck trip limit:**

$$x_T \le 10$$

**(C3) Total trip limit:**

$$x_C + x_T + x_B \le 15$$

**(C4) Bus share constraint** — bus trips ≤ one-fifth of total trips:

$$x_B \le \tfrac{1}{5}\,(x_C + x_T + x_B) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 5x_B \le x_C + x_T + x_B \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 4x_B \le x_C + x_T$$

**(C5) Maximum two modes used:**

$$\sum_{i \in \{C,T,B\}} y_i \le 2$$

**(C6) Linking constraints** — mode used iff at least one trip (with big-M):

$$x_i \le M\,y_i \qquad \forall i \in \{C, T, B\}$$

**(C7) Variable domains:**

$$x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \qquad y_i \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall i \in \{C, T, B\}$$

## 6. Assumptions (marked as such)

1. **Trip counts are integers** (a "trip" is indivisible). *(Assumption: no fractional trips.)*
2. **"Maximum two modes" means at most two modes may have a positive trip count** — modeled via the binary $y_i$ and C5/C6. *(Assumption: using zero trips of a mode is equivalent to not selecting it.)*
3. **The one-fifth bus rule is applied to the realized total number of trips** (not to a fixed upper bound). *(Assumption: interpretation of "total number of trips.")*
4. **Big-M value $M = 15$** is valid because C3 bounds every $x_i$ by 15. *(Assumption: consistent with the trip cap.)*
5. **No minimum trip requirement per selected mode** other than $x_i \ge 1$ when $y_i = 1$ (implied by C6 and the objective structure). *(Assumption.)*
6. **Pollution and capacity are linear and additive** across trips. *(Assumption: standard linearity.)*
7. **All trips are identical within a mode** (same pollution and capacity). *(Assumption.)*

## 7. Complete Model (compact form)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & Z = 100x_C + 80x_T + 110x_B \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& 25x_C + 30x_T + 40x_B \ge 500 \\
& x_T \le 10 \\
& x_C + x_T + x_B \le 15 \\
& 4x_B \le x_C + x_T \\
& y_C + y_T + y_B \le 2 \\
& x_i \le 15\,y_i, \quad \forall i \in \{C,T,B\} \\
& x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \; y_i \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall i \in \{C,T,B\}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 8. Illustrative Feasible Solution Check

Using only cars and trucks ($y_B = 0$): e.g., $x_C = 8$, $x_T = 10$ gives capacity $25(8)+30(10)=500$, total trips $18 > 15$ — infeasible. Try $x_C = 12$, $x_T = 7$: capacity $300 + 210 = 510 \ge 500$, trips $= 19 > 15$ — infeasible. Try $x_C = 10$, $x_T = 9$: capacity $250 + 270 = 520$, trips $= 19$ — infeasible. The binding trip cap (C3) combined with C4 makes the feasible set tight; the solver will identify the optimal mix (e.g., a car–bus or truck–bus combination satisfying $4x_B \le x_C + x_T$). This confirms the model captures the intended trade-offs.

# MILP: Transportation Mode Selection Minimizing Pollution

Below is the implementation in **Python (PuLP)** and **GAMS**.

---

## Python (PuLP)

```python
"""
MILP: Transportation Mode Selection Minimizing Pollution
Modes: car, truck, bus
"""

import pulp

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
model = pulp.LpProblem("Transport_Mode_Selection", pulp.LpMinimize)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Sets / Indices
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
modes = ["car", "truck", "bus"]

# Pollution coefficients per trip
pollution = {"car": 100, "truck": 80, "bus": 110}

# Capacity per trip
capacity = {"car": 25, "truck": 30, "bus": 40}

M = 15  # Big-M = max total trips

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Decision Variables
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# x_i >= 0 integer : number of trips using mode i
x = {i: pulp.LpVariable(f"x_{i}", lowBound=0, cat=pulp.LpInteger) for i in modes}

# y_i in {0,1} : 1 if mode i is used
y = {i: pulp.LpVariable(f"y_{i}", cat=pulp.LpBinary) for i in modes}

# z_i in {0,1} : 1 if mode i is NOT selected
z = {i: pulp.LpVariable(f"z_{i}", cat=pulp.LpBinary) for i in modes}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Objective: minimize total pollution
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
model += pulp.lpSum(pollution[i] * x[i] for i in modes), "Total_Pollution"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Constraints
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# (1) Capacity: total capacity >= 500
model += pulp.lpSum(capacity[i] * x[i] for i in modes) >= 500, "Capacity"

# (2) Truck limit
model += x["truck"] <= 10, "Truck_Limit"

# (3) Total trips <= 15
model += pulp.lpSum(x[i] for i in modes) <= 15, "Total_Trips"

# (4) Bus fraction: 5*x_bus <= x_car + x_truck + x_bus
model += 5 * x["bus"] <= pulp.lpSum(x[i] for i in modes), "Bus_Fraction"

# (5) At most two modes: sum_i y_i <= 2
model += pulp.lpSum(y[i] for i in modes) <= 2, "At_Most_Two_Modes"

# (6) Linking: x_i <= M * y_i
for i in modes:
    model += x[i] <= M * y[i], f"Link_{i}"

# (7) Consistency: z_i = 1 - y_i  (z_i is 1 if mode i is NOT selected)
for i in modes:
    model += y[i] + z[i] == 1, f"Not_Selected_{i}"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Solve
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
model.solve(pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=1))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Report
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("\nStatus:", pulp.LpStatus[model.status])
print("Minimum Total Pollution =", pulp.value(model.objective))

print("\n--- Trips (x_i) ---")
for i in modes:
    print(f"  x_{i:5s} = {int(round(x[i].value()))}")

print("\n--- Mode Used (y_i) ---")
for i in modes:
    print(f"  y_{i:5s} = {int(round(y[i].value()))}")

print("\n--- Mode NOT Used (z_i) ---")
for i in modes:
    print(f"  z_{i:5s} = {int(round(z[i].value()))}")

# Verify capacity
total_cap = sum(capacity[i] * int(round(x[i].value())) for i in modes)
print(f"\nTotal capacity delivered = {total_cap} (>= 500 required)")
```

- `y_i ∈ {0,1}` — 1 if mode i is used, 0 otherwise
- `z_i ∈ {0,1}` — 1 if mode i is **not** selected, 0 otherwise (auxiliary)

Minimize total pollution:

$$\min \; Z = 100\,x_{car} + 80\,x_{truck} + 110\,x_{bus}$$

**(3) Total trips limit:**

**(4) Bus fraction** — bus trips ≤ one-fifth of total trips:

equivalently:
$$5\,x_{bus} \leq x_{car} + x_{truck} + x_{bus}$$

**(5) At most two modes selected:**
$$\sum_{i} y_i \leq 2$$

**(6) Linking constraints** — trips only allowed if mode is selected (Big-M):
$$x_i \leq M \cdot y_i \quad \forall i \in \{car, truck, bus\}$$

**(7) Mode-selection consistency:**
$$y_i + z_i = 1 \quad \forall i \in \{car, truck, bus\}$$

**(8) Variable domains:**
$$x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, \quad y_i, z_i \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall i$$

messages.content:
# MILP: Transportation Mode Selection and Trip Planning

## Decision Variables

**Integer trip counts** (non-negative integers):
- $x_{\text{car}} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ — number of car trips
- $x_{\text{truck}} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ — number of truck trips
- $x_{\text{bus}} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ — number of bus trips

**Binary mode-use indicators:**
- $y_{\text{car}} \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if cars are used, 0 otherwise
- $y_{\text{truck}} \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if trucks are used, 0 otherwise
- $y_{\text{bus}} \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if buses are used, 0 otherwise

## Objective Function

Minimize total pollution:

$$\min \; 100\,x_{\text{car}} + 80\,x_{\text{truck}} + 110\,x_{\text{bus}}$$

## Constraints

**1. Demand satisfaction** (at least 500 units delivered):

$$25\,x_{\text{car}} + 30\,x_{\text{truck}} + 40\,x_{\text{bus}} \geq 500$$

**2. Mode linking** (a mode can carry trips only if selected; big-M bounded by the total-trip cap of 15, and 10 for trucks):

$$x_{\text{car}} \leq 15\,y_{\text{car}}$$
$$x_{\text{truck}} \leq 10\,y_{\text{truck}}$$
$$x_{\text{bus}} \leq 15\,y_{\text{bus}}$$

**3. At most two of the three modes may be used:**

$$y_{\text{car}} + y_{\text{truck}} + y_{\text{bus}} \leq 2$$

**4. Truck trip limit:**

$$x_{\text{truck}} \leq 10$$

**5. Bus fraction** (bus trips ≤ one-fifth of total trips):

$$5\,x_{\text{bus}} \leq x_{\text{car}} + x_{\text{truck}} + x_{\text{bus}}$$

Equivalently: $4\,x_{\text{bus}} \leq x_{\text{car}} + x_{\text{truck}}$.

**6. Total trip cap:**

$$x_{\text{car}} + x_{\text{truck}} + x_{\text{bus}} \leq 15$$

**7. Variable domains:**

$$x_{\text{car}}, x_{\text{truck}}, x_{\text{bus}} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, \qquad y_{\text{car}}, y_{\text{truck}}, y_{\text{bus}} \in \{0,1\}$$

---

## Explanation of Model Elements

**Decision variables.** The integer variables $x_m$ count how many trips each mode makes; the binary variables $y_m$ act as on/off switches that record whether a mode is used at all. The two layers are tied together by the linking constraints, which is what makes this a *mixed-integer* program.

**Objective.** Each trip of a given mode contributes a fixed pollution amount (car 100, truck 80, bus 110 per trip). Because pollution is additive and linear in trip counts, the objective is a plain linear sum to be minimized.

**Demand constraint (1).** Each mode moves a fixed number of units per trip (25/30/40). The weighted sum must reach the 500-unit requirement. This is the only constraint forcing positive activity, so it drives the solution.

**Mode-linking constraints (2).** These enforce the logical implication "$x_m > 0 \Rightarrow y_m = 1$." Model 1:
# Mixed-Integer Linear Program: Transportation Mode Selection

## Decision Variables

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| $x_C$ | Integer ≥ 0 | Number of **car** trips |
| $x_T$ | Integer ≥ 0 | Number of **truck** trips |
| $x_B$ | Integer ≥ 0 | Number of **bus** trips |
| $y_C$ | Binary | 1 if **car** mode is used, 0 otherwise |
| $y_T$ | Binary | 1 if **truck** mode is used, 0 otherwise |
| $y_B$ | Binary | 1 if **bus** mode is used, 0 otherwise |

## Objective Function

Minimize total pollution:

$$\min \; Z = 100\,x_C + 80\,x_T + 110\,x_B$$

## Constraints

**(1) Delivery requirement** — at least 500 units:
$$25\,x_C + 30\,x_T + 40\,x_B \ge 500$$

**(2) Truck trip limit** — at most 10 truck trips:
$$x_T \le 10$$

**(3) Bus share limit** — bus trips ≤ 1/5 of total trips:
$$x_B \le \tfrac{1}{5}\,(x_C + x_T + x_B) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 4\,x_B - x_C - x_T \le 0$$

**(4) Total trip limit** — at most 15 trips:
$$x_C + x_T + x_B \le 15$$

**(5) Mode-usage linking** — a mode can carry trips only if its indicator is on (big-M with $M = 15$, the trip cap):
$$x_C \le 15\,y_C, \qquad x_T \le 15\,y_T, \qquad x_B \le 15\,y_B$$

**(6) At most 2 of 3 modes used:**
$$y_C + y_T + y_B \le 2$$

**(7) Variable domains:**
$$x_C, x_T, x_B \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \qquad y_C, y_T, y_B \in \{0,1\}$$

## Explanation of Model Elements

- **Objective:** Each trip's pollution is linear in the number of trips, so total pollution is a weighted sum. Minimizing it favors trucks (80/trip) over cars (100) and buses (110), but capacity and the mode-count limit force trade-offs.
- **Delivery constraint (1):** Ensures the 500-unit requirement; capacities (25/30/40) make buses the most efficient per trip, so the bus-share cap (3) is binding in tension with this.
- **Truck cap (2):** A direct upper bound on $x_T$ independent of the mode indicator.
- **Bus-share constraint (3):** Written in linear form $4x_B - x_C - x_T \le 0$ to avoid division; it prevents relying too heavily on buses.
- **Trip cap (4):** Combined with capacity, it bounds the feasible region (e.g., 15 cars give only 375 units, so some trucks/buses are needed).

- **Mode-count constraint (6):** The "at most 2 of 3 modes" restriction; it is what makes the binaries essential rather than redundant.
- **Integrality:** Trip counts are whole trips; indicators are binary. This is a genuine MILP (the LP relaxation would allow fractional trips and fractional mode use).

A solver (e.g., CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX) will return the optimal trip mix and the minimum achievable pollution.

Model 2:
Here is a complete linear MILP formulation for the described problem.

## Sets and Indices

- Let the transportation modes be indexed by \(m \in \{C, T, B\}\), where:
  - \(C\) = car
  - \(T\) = truck
  - \(B\) = bus

## Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Car \(C\) | Truck \(T\) | Bus \(B\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(c_m\) | Capacity per trip (units) | 25 | 30 | 40 |
| \(p_m\) | Pollution per trip | 100 | 80 | 110 |
| \(U_m\) | Maximum number of trips | \(\infty\) | 10 | \(\infty\) |

Other parameters:
- Minimum total delivered units: \(D = 500\)
- Maximum total trips: \(N_{\max} = 15\)
- Maximum number of modes used: \(K = 2\)
- Bus share limit: bus trips \(\le \frac{1}{5}\) of total trips

## Decision Variables

- \(x_m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\): number of trips using mode \(m\) (integer)
- \(y_m \in \{0,1\}\): binary indicator equal to 1 if mode \(m\) is used (i.e., \(x_m > 0\)), 0 otherwise

## Objective Function

Minimize total pollution:

\[
\min \; Z = 100\,x_C + 80\,x_T + 110\,x_B
\]

## Constraints

**(1) Demand satisfaction** — at least 500 units delivered:

\[
25\,x_C + 30\,x_T + 40\,x_B \ge 500
\]

**(2) Truck trip limit**:

\[
x_T \le 10
\]

**(3) Total trips limit**:

\[
x_C + x_T + x_B \le 15
\]

**(4) Bus share constraint** — bus trips at most one-fifth of total trips:

\[
x_B \le \tfrac{1}{5}\,(x_C + x_T + x_B)
\]

Equivalently (multiplying by 5 to avoid fractions):

\[
5\,x_B \le x_C + x_T + x_B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
4\,x_B \le x_C + x_T
\]

**(5) Mode-use linking** — a mode can carry trips only if selected:

\[
x_m \le U_m^{\text{big}}\, y_m \quad \forall m \in \{C, T, B\}
\]

where \(U_m^{\text{big}}\) is a valid upper bound on trips of mode \(m\). A safe choice is \(U_m^{\text{big}} = 15\) for all modes (since total trips \(\le 15\)); for trucks one may use 10.

**(6) At most 2 of the 3 modes selected**:

\[
y_C + y_T + y_B \le 2
\]

**(7) Variable domains**:

\[
x_C, x_T, x_B \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \qquad y_C, y_T, y_B \in \{0,1\}
\]

## Explanation of Model Elements

- **Objective (pollution minimization):** Each trip contributes a fixed pollution amount depending on mode; the linear objective sums these contributions. Since all coefficients are positive, the solver naturally avoids unnecessary trips.

- **Demand constraint:** Ensures the fleet of trips collectively transports at least 500 units. It is a covering (≥) constraint because over-delivery is allowed.

- **Truck limit (\(x_T \le 10\)):** A direct upper bound reflecting the stated maximum of 10 truck trips.

- **Total trips limit:** Caps the fleet size at 15 trips, coupling all three modes.

- **Bus share constraint:** The form \(x_B \le \frac{1}{5}(x_C+x_T+x_B)\) is linear once multiplied through; the equivalent \(4x_B \le x_C + x_T\) is preferred numerically. It forces enough non-bus trips whenever buses are used.

- **Mode-use linking:** The big-M constraints \(x_m \le U_m^{\text{big}} y_m\) tie the integer trip count to the binary indicator. If \(y_m = 0\), then \(x_m = 0\); if \(y_m = 1\), trips up to the bound are allowed. This is what makes the "at most 2 modes" restriction meaningful.

- **Cardinality constraint (\(y_C+y_T+y_B \le 2\)):** Enforces that at most two of the three transportation modes are actually used, exactly as required.

- **Integrality:** Trip counts are integer (you cannot run a fraction of a trip), and mode indicators are binary.

## Compact Summary

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & 100x_C + 80x_T + 110x_B \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& 25x_C + 30x_T + 40x_B \ge 500 \\
& x_T \le 10 \\
& x_C + x_T + x_B \le 15 \\
& 4x_B \le x_C + x_T \\
& x_C \le 15y_C,\quad x_T \le 10y_T,\quad x_B \le 15y_B \\
& y_C + y_T + y_B \le 2 \\
& x_C, x_T, x_B \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, \quad y_C, y_T, y_B \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

This is a linear MILP: the objective and all constraints are linear in the variables, with integrality on trip counts and binary mode-selection indicators.

# Production Planning MILP with Quantity-Dependent Profit Margins

## 1. Problem Summary

A factory produces products A, B, and C using three resources: technical preparation time, direct labor, and material. Profit per unit depends on the sales volume bracket (bulk discounts reduce unit profit as volume grows). We must decide production quantities to maximize total profit.

**Assumption (marked):** All production is sold (no inventory), and production quantities are continuous (LP relaxation of integer units). This keeps the model linear. If integer units are required, the same model applies with integrality on the quantity variables.

---

## 2. Parameters

### Resource requirements per unit

| Resource | A | B | C | Available |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Technical preparation (h) | 1 | 2 | 1 | 100 |
| Direct labor (h) | 10 | 4 | 5 | 700 |
| Material (kg) | 3 | 2 | 1 | 400 |

### Profit brackets (yuan/unit) — piecewise-decreasing unit profit

**Product A** (brackets: 0–40, 40–100, 100–150, >150):

| Segment $k$ | Range (units) | Width $w^A_k$ | Unit profit $p^A_k$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0–40 | 40 | 10 |
| 2 | 40–100 | 60 | 9 |
| 3 | 100–150 | 50 | 8 |
| 4 | >150 | $M_A$ (large) | 7 |

**Product B** (brackets: 0–50, 50–100, >100):

| Segment $k$ | Range (units) | Width $w^B_k$ | Unit profit $p^B_k$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0–50 | 50 | 6 |
| 2 | 50–100 | 50 | 4 |
| 3 | >100 | $M_B$ (large) | 3 |

**Product C** (brackets: 0–100, >100):

| Segment $k$ | Range (units) | Width $w^C_k$ | Unit profit $p^C_k$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0–100 | 100 | 5 |
| 2 | >100 | $M_C$ (large) | 4 |

**Assumption (marked):** The last (open-ended) bracket is bounded by a sufficiently large number $M_j$ so the model stays finite. A valid bound is the maximum producible quantity from resources, e.g. $M_j = \min\{\text{tech limit}, \text{labor limit}, \text{material limit}\}$ for that product. For product A: $\min(100, 70, 133) = 70$; product B: $\min(50, 175, 200) = 50$; product C: $\min(100, 140, 400) = 100$. To be safe, use $M_A = 200$, $M_B = 200$, $M_C = 400$ (larger than any feasible quantity).

---

## 3. Decision Variables

Let $j \in \{A, B, C\}$ and $k$ index the profit segments.

- $x_{jk} \ge 0$: quantity of product $j$ sold in segment $k$ (units).
- $y_{jk} \in \{0,1\}$: binary indicator that segment $k$ of product $j$ is used.

Total quantity of product $j$:
$$Q_j = \sum_k x_{jk}$$

---

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total profit:

$$\max Z = \sum_{j}\sum_{k} p_{jk}\, x_{jk}$$

Explicitly:
$$\max Z = 10x_{A1} + 9x_{A2} + 8x_{A3} + 7x_{A4} + 6x_{B1} + 4x_{B2} + 3x_{B3} + 5x_{C1} + 4x_{C2}$$

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Resource constraints

Technical preparation:
$$1\cdot Q_A + 2\cdot Q_B + 1\cdot Q_C \le 100$$

Direct labor:
$$10\cdot Q_A + 4\cdot Q_B + 5\cdot Q_C \le 700$$

Material:
$$3\cdot Q_A + 2\cdot Q_B + 1\cdot Q_C \le 400$$

where $Q_A = x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}$, etc.

### 5.2 Segment capacity constraints (with binary activation)

For each product, segment $k$ can only be filled if all previous segments are filled (ordered filling), and each segment is bounded by its width.

**Product A:**
$$x_{A1} \le 40\, y_{A1}$$
$$x_{A2} \le 60\, y_{A2}, \quad x_{A2} \ge 60\, y_{A2} - 60\,(1-y_{A1})\ \text{(see note)}$$
$$x_{A3} \le 50\, y_{A3}$$
$$x_{A4} \le M_A\, y_{A4}$$

**Product B:**
$$x_{B1} \le 50\, y_{B1}$$
$$x_{B2} \le 50\, y_{B2}$$
$$x_{B3} \le M_B\, y_{B3}$$

**Product C:**
$$x_{C1} \le 100\, y_{C1}$$
$$x_{C2} \le M_C\, y_{C2}$$

### 5.3 Ordered-filling (precedence) constraints

To ensure the piecewise profit is correctly applied (you cannot use a later, cheaper bracket unless earlier brackets are full):

$$y_{A2} \le y_{A1}, \quad y_{A3} \le y_{A2}, \quad y_{A4} \le y_{A3}$$
$$y_{B2} \le y_{B1}, \quad y_{B3} \le y_{B2}$$
$$y_{C2} \le y_{C1}$$

### 5.4 Lower-bound (fill) constraints for intermediate segments

When a segment is activated, it must be filled to its full width (so the bracket structure is exact). For product A:

$$x_{A1} \ge 40\, y_{A1}$$
$$x_{A2} \ge 60\, y_{A2}$$
$$x_{A3} \ge 50\, y_{A3}$$
$$x_{A4} \ge 0 \quad (\text{last segment, no lower bound beyond activation})$$

Similarly for B:
$$x_{B1} \ge 50\, y_{B1}, \quad x_{B2} \ge 50\, y_{B2}, \quad x_{B3} \ge 0$$

For C:
$$x_{C1} \ge 100\, y_{C1}, \quad x_{C2} \ge 0$$

**Assumption (marked):** This "all-or-nothing per bracket" formulation is the standard exact linearization of a decreasing piecewise unit-profit function. It forces intermediate brackets to be completely filled before the next bracket is used. (An alternative relaxation without lower bounds would allow "cherry-picking" cheaper brackets, which is not economically meaningful.)

### 5.5 Binary and non-negativity

$$y_{jk} \in \{0,1\}, \quad x_{jk} \ge 0$$

---

## 6. Complete Model (compact form)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\ Z = &\ 10x_{A1}+9x_{A2}+8x_{A3}+7x_{A4}\\
&+6x_{B1}+4x_{B2}+3x_{B3}\\
&+5x_{C1}+4x_{C2}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}\quad
& (x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}) + 2(x_{B1}+x_{B2}+x_{B3}) + (x_{C1}+x_{C2}) \le 100\\
& 10(x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}) + 4(x_{B1}+x_{B2}+x_{B3}) + 5(x_{C1}+x_{C2}) \le 700\\
& 3(x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}) + 2(x_{B1}+x_{B2}+x_{B3}) + (x_{C1}+x_{C2}) \le 400\\[4pt]
& 40y_{A1} \le x_{A1} \le 40y_{A1}\\
& 60y_{A2} \le x_{A2} \le 60y_{A2}\\
& 50y_{A3} \le x_{A3} \le 50y_{A3}\\
& 0 \le x_{A4} \le M_A y_{A4}\\
& 50y_{B1} \le x_{B1} \le 50y_{B1}\\
& 50y_{B2} \le x_{B2} \le 50y_{B2}\\
& 0 \le x_{B3} \le M_B y_{B3}\\
& 100y_{C1} \le x_{C1} \le 100y_{C1}\\
& 0 \le x_{C2} \le M_C y_{C2}\\[4pt]
& y_{A2}\le y_{A1},\ y_{A3}\le y_{A2},\ y_{A4}\le y_{A3}\\
& y_{B2}\le y_{B1},\ y_{B3}\le y_{B2}\\
& y_{C2}\le y_{C1}\\[4pt]
& x_{jk}\ge 0,\quad y_{jk}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 7. Assumptions (explicitly marked)

1. **Continuous quantities.** Units are treated as continuous; if integer output is required, add $x_{jk}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.
2. **All output sold.** No inventory or unmet demand; production = sales.
3. **Exact bracket filling.** Intermediate brackets must be filled completely before moving to the next (standard piecewise-linear exact formulation). This is enforced by the lower-bound constraints $x_{jk}\ge w_{jk}y_{jk}$ for non-final segments.
4. **Finite last bracket.** Open-ended brackets are capped by sufficiently large $M_j$ ($M_A=200$, $M_B=200$, $M_C=400$), larger than any resource-feasible quantity.
5. **No setup costs or changeover times** beyond the stated per-unit resource requirements.
6. **Profit is revenue minus variable cost**, already net, and depends only on the bracket of the total quantity sold for that product.

---

## 8. Model Size

- Continuous variables: 9 ($x$)
- Binary variables: 9 ($y$)
- Constraints: 3 resource + 9 upper-bound + 6 lower-bound (non-final segments) + 6 precedence = 24 (plus non-negativity).

This is a small MILP solvable by any standard solver (e.g., CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX). The optimal plan will fill the most profitable brackets first (A up to 40 at 10 yuan, then B up to 50 at 6 yuan, C up to 100 at 5 yuan, etc.) subject to the three shared resource limits.

| Direct labor (h) | 10 | 4 | 5 | 700 |
| Material (kg) | 3 | 2 | 1 | 400 |

### Profit brackets (yuan/unit) — piecewise-decreasing unit profit

**Product A** (brackets: 0–40, 40–100, 100–150, >150):

| Segment $k$ | Range (units) | Width $w^A_k$ | Unit profit $p^A_k$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0–40 | 40 | 10 |
| 2 | 40–100 | 60 | 9 |
| 3 | 100–150 | 50 | 8 |
| 4 | >150 | $M_A$ (large) | 7 |

**Product B** (brackets: 0–50, 50–100, >100):

| Segment $k$ | Range (units) | Width $w^B_k$ | Unit profit $p^B_k$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0–50 | 50 | 6 |
| 2 | 50–100 | 50 | 4 |
| 3 | >100 | $M_B$ (large) | 3 |

**Product C** (brackets: 0–100, >100):

| Segment $k$ | Range (units) | Width $w^C_k$ | Unit profit $p^C_k$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0–100 | 100 | 5 |
| 2 | >100 | $M_C$ (large) | 4 |

**Assumption (marked):** The last (open-ended) bracket is bounded by a sufficiently large number $M_j$ so the model stays finite. A valid bound is the maximum producible quantity from resources, e.g. $M_j = \min\{\text{tech limit}, \text{labor limit}, \text{material limit}\}$ for that product. For product A: $\min(100, 70, 133) = 70$; product B: $\min(50, 175, 200) = 50$; product C: $\min(100, 140, 400) = 100$. To be safe, use $M_A = 200$, $M_B = 200$, $M_C = 400$ (larger than any feasible quantity).

---

## 3. Decision Variables

Let $j \in \{A, B, C\}$ and $k$ index the profit segments.

- $x_{jk} \ge 0$: quantity of product $j$ sold in segment $k$ (units).
- $y_{jk} \in \{0,1\}$: binary indicator that segment $k$ of product $j$ is used.

Total quantity of product $j$:
$$Q_j = \sum_k x_{jk}$$

---

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total profit:

$$\max Z = \sum_{j}\sum_{k} p_{jk}\, x_{jk}$$

Explicitly:
$$\max Z = 10x_{A1} + 9x_{A2} + 8x_{A3} + 7x_{A4} + 6x_{B1} + 4x_{B2} + 3x_{B3} + 5x_{C1} + 4x_{C2}$$

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Resource constraints

Technical preparation:
$$1\cdot Q_A + 2\cdot Q_B + 1\cdot Q_C \le 100$$

Direct labor:
$$10\cdot Q_A + 4\cdot Q_B + 5\cdot Q_C \le 700$$

Material:
$$3\cdot Q_A + 2\cdot Q_B + 1\cdot Q_C \le 400$$

where $Q_A = x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}$, etc.

### 5.2 Segment capacity constraints (with binary activation)

For each product, segment $k$ can only be filled if all previous segments are filled (ordered filling), and each segment is bounded by its width.

**Product A:**
$$x_{A1} \le 40\, y_{A1}$$
$$x_{A2} \le 60\, y_{A2}, \quad x_{A2} \ge 60\, y_{A2} - 60\,(1-y_{A1})\ \text{(see note)}$$
$$x_{A3} \le 50\, y_{A3}$$
$$x_{A4} \le M_A\, y_{A4}$$

**Product B:**
$$x_{B1} \le 50\, y_{B1}$$
$$x_{B2} \le 50\, y_{B2}$$
$$x_{B3} \le M_B\, y_{B3}$$

**Product C:**
$$x_{C1} \le 100\, y_{C1}$$
$$x_{C2} \le M_C\, y_{C2}$$

### 5.3 Ordered-filling (precedence) constraints

To ensure the piecewise profit is correctly applied (you cannot use a later, cheaper bracket unless earlier brackets are full):

$$y_{A2} \le y_{A1}, \quad y_{A3} \le y_{A2}, \quad y_{A4} \le y_{A3}$$
$$y_{B2} \le y_{B1}, \quad y_{B3} \le y_{B2}$$
$$y_{C2} \le y_{C1}$$

### 5.4 Lower-bound (fill) constraints for intermediate segments

When a segment is activated, it must be filled to its full width (so the bracket structure is exact). For product A:

$$x_{A1} \ge 40\, y_{A1}$$
$$x_{A2} \ge 60\, y_{A2}$$
$$x_{A3} \ge 50\, y_{A3}$$
$$x_{A4} \ge 0 \quad (\text{last segment, no lower bound beyond activation})$$

Similarly for B:
$$x_{B1} \ge 50\, y_{B1}, \quad x_{B2} \ge 50\, y_{B2}, \quad x_{B3} \ge 0$$

For C:
$$x_{C1} \ge 100\, y_{C1}, \quad x_{C2} \ge 0$$

**Assumption (marked):** This "all-or-nothing per bracket" formulation is the standard exact linearization of a decreasing piecewise unit-profit function. It forces intermediate brackets to be completely filled before the next bracket is used. (An alternative relaxation without lower bounds would allow "cherry-picking" cheaper brackets, which is not economically meaningful.)

### 5.5 Binary and non-negativity

$$y_{jk} \in \{0,1\}, \quad x_{jk} \ge 0$$

---

## 6. Complete Model (compact form)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\ Z = &\ 10x_{A1}+9x_{A2}+8x_{A3}+7x_{A4}\\
&+6x_{B1}+4x_{B2}+3x_{B3}\\
&+5x_{C1}+4x_{C2}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}\quad
& (x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}) + 2(x_{B1}+x_{B2}+x_{B3}) + (x_{C1}+x_{C2}) \le 100\\
& 10(x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}) + 4(x_{B1}+x_{B2}+x_{B3}) + 5(x_{C1}+x_{C2}) \le 700\\
& 3(x_{A1}+x_{A2}+x_{A3}+x_{A4}) + 2(x_{B1}+x_{B2}+x_{B3}) + (x_{C1}+x_{C2}) \le 400\\[4pt]
& 40y_{A1} \le x_{A1} \le 40y_{A1}\\
& 60y_{A2} \le x_{A2} \le 60y_{A2}\\
& 50y_{A3} \le x_{A3} \le 50y_{A3}\\
& 0 \le x_{A4} \le M_A y_{A4}\\
& 50y_{B1} \le x_{B1} \le 50y_{B1}\\
& 50y_{B2} \le x_{B2} \le 50y_{B2}\\
& 0 \le x_{B3} \le M_B y_{B3}\\
& 100y_{C1} \le x_{C1} \le 100y_{C1}\\
& 0 \le x_{C2} \le M_C y_{C2}\\[4pt]
& y_{A2}\le y_{A1},\ y_{A3}\le y_{A2},\ y_{A4}\le y_{A3}\\
& y_{B2}\le y_{B1},\ y_{B3}\le y_{B2}\\
& y_{C2}\le y_{C1}\\[4pt]
& x_{jk}\ge 0,\quad y_{jk}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 7. Assumptions (explicitly marked)

1. **Continuous quantities.** Units are treated as continuous; if integer output is required, add $x_{jk}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.
2. **All output sold.** No inventory or unmet demand; production = sales.
3. **Exact bracket filling.** Intermediate brackets must be filled completely before moving to the next (standard piecewise-linear exact formulation). This is enforced by the lower-bound constraints $x_{jk}\ge w_{jk}y_{jk}$ for non-final segments.
4. **Finite last bracket.** Open-ended brackets are capped by sufficiently large $M_j$ ($M_A=200$, $M_B=200$, $M_C=400$), larger than any resource-feasible quantity.
5. **No setup costs or changeover times** beyond the stated per-unit resource requirements.
6. **Profit is revenue minus variable cost**, already net, and depends only on the bracket of the total quantity sold for that product.

---

## 8. Model Size

- Continuous variables: 9 ($x$)
- Binary variables: 9 ($y$)
- Constraints: 3 resource + 9 upper-bound + 6 lower-bound (non-final segments) + 6 precedence = 24 (plus non-negativity).

This is a small MILP solvable by any standard solver (e.g., CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX). The optimal plan will fill the most profitable brackets first (A up to 40 at 10 yuan, then B up to 50 at 6 yuan, C up to 100 at 5 yuan, etc.) subject to the three shared resource limits.

response.content:
# MILP Model: Production Planning with Quantity-Discount Profit Tiers

## 1. Sets and Indices

- Products: $p \in \{A, B, C\}$
- Resources: $r \in \{\text{prep}, \text{labor}, \text{material}\}$
- Tiers per product: $t \in T_p$, where $T_A=\{1,2,3,4\}$, $T_B=\{1,2,3\}$, $T_C=\{1,2\}$

## 2. Parameters (Data)

**Resource use per unit** $a_{pr}$ (prep hours, labor hours, material kg):

| Product | prep | labor | material |
|---------|------|-------|----------|
| A | 1 | 10 | 3 |
| B | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| C | 1 | 5 | 1 |

**Resource availability** $b_r$: $\quad b_{\text{prep}} = 100$, $\quad b_{\text{labor}} = 700$, $\quad b_{\text{material}} = 400$

**Tier structure** — lower/upper bounds and marginal profit $c_{pt}$:

| Product | Tier | Range | Marginal profit $c_{pt}$ | Width $w_{pt}$ |
|---------|------|-------|--------------------------|----------------|
| A | 1 | 0–40 | 10 | 40 |
| A | 2 | 40–100 | 9 | 60 |
| A | 3 | 100–150 | 8 | 50 |
| A | 4 | 150–∞ | 7 | $M_A$ |
| B | 1 | 0–50 | 6 | 50 |
| B | 2 | 50–100 | 4 | 50 |
| B | 3 | 100–∞ | 3 | $M_B$ |
| C | 1 | 0–100 | 5 | 100 |
| C | 2 | 100–∞ | 4 | $M_C$ |

**Big-M** (tightest resource bound per product): $M_p = \min_r \lfloor b_r / a_{pr} \rfloor$, giving $M_A = 70$, $M_B = 50$, $M_C = 100$. *(Assumption: production quantities are continuous; if integrality of units is required, treat $y_{pt}$ as integer.)*

## 3. Decision Variables

- $y_{pt} \ge 0$ — incremental quantity of product $p$ produced/sold in tier $t$ (beyond the tier's lower bound), with $y_{pt} \le w_{pt}$.
- $z_{pt} \in \{0,1\}$ — binary indicator: 1 if tier $t$ of product $p$ is "opened" (used).

Total production of product $p$: $\; x_p = \sum_{t \in T_p} y_{pt}$.

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total profit (sum of marginal profit × incremental quantity over all tiers):

$$\max \; Z = \sum_{p}\sum_{t \in T_p} c_{pt}\, y_{pt}$$

## 5. Constraints

**(1) Resource capacity constraints** (for each resource $r$):

$$\sum_{p}\sum_{t \in T_p} a_{pr}\, y_{pt} \;\le\; b_r \qquad \forall r$$

**(2) Tier capacity** (a tier's incremental quantity cannot exceed its width, and is zero unless the tier is opened):

$$y_{pt} \;\le\; w_{pt}\, z_{pt} \qquad \forall p,\ \forall t \in T_p$$

**(3) Tier ordering** (tier $t$ can only be opened if tier $t-1$ is opened):

$$z_{pt} \;\le\; z_{p,t-1} \qquad \forall p,\ \forall t \in T_p,\ t \ge 2$$

**(4) Tier fullness** (tier $t-1$ must be completely filled before tier $t$ can be opened):

$$y_{p,t-1} \;\ge\; w_{p,t-1}\, z_{pt} \qquad \forall p,\ \forall t \in T_p,\ t \ge 2$$

**(5) Variable domains:**

$$y_{pt} \ge 0, \qquad z_{pt} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Modeling Notes / Assumptions

- **Concave, decreasing marginal profit.** Because profit per unit decreases as volume grows, the incremental (delta) formulation with the "fullness" constraint (4) exactly reproduces the piecewise-constant marginal profit table; the LP relaxation is naturally tight.
- **"Sales volume" = production.** *Assumption:* everything produced is sold, so production quantity equals sales volume (no inventory, no demand cap beyond the tier structure).
- **Top tier is unbounded** in the table; it is bounded in the model by the tightest resource limit $M_p$, which is a valid (non-restrictive) bound since no product can exceed it.
- **Continuous quantities** are assumed. If whole units are required, declare $y_{pt}$ integer (the model remains a valid MILP).
- The binary $z_{p,1}$ needs no ordering constraint (first tier is always available); it is only linked through capacity constraint (2).

messages.content:
# MILP Formulation: Production Planning with Quantity-Discount Profit

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $i \in I = \{A, B, C\}$ | Products |
| $k \in K_i$ | Price segments for product $i$ (ordered from lowest to highest volume) |

Segment definitions:

- $K_A = \{1,2,3,4\}$, $K_B = \{1,2,3\}$, $K_C = \{1,2\}$

## 2. Parameters

### Resource coefficients $r_{i,\ell}$ (per unit of product $i$)

| Product | Tech. prep (h) | Labor (h) | Material (kg) |
|---------|---------------|-----------|---------------|
| A | 1 | 10 | 3 |
| B | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| C | 1 | 5 | 1 |

### Resource availability $R_\ell$

- Technical preparation: $R_{\text{tech}} = 100$
- Labor: $R_{\text{lab}} = 700$
- Material: $R_{\text{mat}} = 400$

### Segment bounds and unit profits

For each product $i$ and segment $k$, let $[L_{ik}, U_{ik}]$ be the volume interval and $p_{ik}$ the unit profit (constant within the segment):

**Product A** ($p_{A,k}$ decreasing):

| $k$ | $L_{Ak}$ | $U_{Ak}$ | $p_{Ak}$ |
|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| 1 | 0 | 40 | 10 |
| 2 | 40 | 100 | 9 |
| 3 | 100 | 150 | 8 |
| 4 | 150 | $\infty$ (use big-$M$) | 7 |

**Product B**:

| $k$ | $L_{Bk}$ | $U_{Bk}$ | $p_{Bk}$ |
|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| 1 | 0 | 50 | 6 |
| 2 | 50 | 100 | 4 |
| 3 | 100 | $\infty$ | 3 |

**Product C**:

| $k$ | $L_{Ck}$ | $U_{Ck}$ | $p_{Ck}$ |
|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| 1 | 0 | 100 | 5 |
| 2 | 100 | $\infty$ | 4 |

### Big-$M$ values

Choose $M_i$ = an upper bound on production of product $i$ implied by resources:

- $M_A = \min(100/1,\; 700/10,\; 400/3) = \min(100, 70, 133.3) = 70$
- $M_B = \min(100/2,\; 700/4,\; 400/2) = \min(50, 175, 200) = 50$
- $M_C = \min(100/1,\; 700/5,\; 400/1) = \min(100, 140, 400) = 100$

**Important observation:** With these resource limits, product A can never exceed 70 units, so segments 3 and 4 of A are unreachable, and product C can never exceed 100 units, so segment 2 of C is unreachable. Product B can reach at most 50 units, so segments 2 and 3 of B are unreachable. To keep the model general and faithful to the stated schedule, we keep all segments but use $M_i$ as the upper bound in the last segment. (In practice you could drop unreachable segments; the model below remains correct either way.)

## 3. Decision Variables

### Production quantities
- $x_i \ge 0$: total production of product $i$ (continuous).

### Segment variables
- $y_{ik} \ge 0$: quantity of product $i$ produced/sold **within segment $k$** (continuous).
- $z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if segment $k$ of product $i$ is "open" (has positive quantity), 0 otherwise.

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total profit:

$$\max \; Z = \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{k \in K_i} p_{ik}\, y_{ik}$$

Because unit profit is decreasing in $k$, and the ordering constraints below force segments to be filled in order, this correctly represents the piecewise-constant decreasing marginal profit.

## 5. Constraints

### (a) Total production equals sum of segment quantities

$$x_i = \sum_{k \in K_i} y_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

### (b) Segment capacity (linking $y$ and $z$)

$$y_{ik} \le (U_{ik} - L_{ik})\, z_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k \in K_i$$

(For the last segment, $U_{ik}-L_{ik}$ is replaced by $M_i - L_{ik}$.)

### (c) Ordering / fill-in-order constraints (SOS1-style)

Segment $k+1$ can only be used if segment $k$ is fully used:

$$y_{ik} \ge (U_{ik} - L_{ik})\, z_{i,k+1} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k = 1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

Equivalently, in binary form:

$$z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k = 1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

Using **both** (b) and (c) is the standard "incremental" piecewise-linear formulation; (c) ensures the decreasing price schedule is applied in order (you cannot use the cheaper higher-volume price before filling the lower-volume segment).

> **Note on the first segment:** For $k=1$, $L_{i1}=0$, so (b) reads $y_{i1} \le U_{i1} z_{i1}$. The constraint (c) for $k=1$ is $y_{i1} \ge U_{i1} z_{i2}$, which forces segment 1 to be full before segment 2 opens. This is the correct "fill in order" condition.

### (d) Resource capacity constraints

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{tech}}\, x_i \le 100$$

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{lab}}\, x_i \le 700$$

# Corrected MILP: Production Planning with Decreasing Piecewise-Constant Unit Profit

  - $K_A = \{1,2,3,4\}$, $K_B = \{1,2,3\}$, $K_C = \{1,2\}$
- $r \in R = \{\text{tech}, \text{labor}, \text{mat}\}$ — resources

## 2. Parameters

**Resource consumption per unit** $a_{ir}$:

| $i$ | tech | labor | mat |
|-----|------|-------|-----|
| A | 1 | 10 | 3 |
| B | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| C | 1 | 5 | 1 |

**Resource capacities** $b_r$: $b_{\text{tech}} = 100$, $b_{\text{labor}} = 700$, $b_{\text{mat}} = 400$.

**Segment breakpoints** $L_{ik}$, $U_{ik}$ and **unit profits** $p_{ik}$:

| $i$ | $k$ | $L_{ik}$ | $U_{ik}$ | $p_{ik}$ |
|-----|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| A | 1 | 0 | 40 | 10 |
| A | 2 | 40 | 100 | 9 |
| A | 3 | 100 | 150 | 8 |
| A | 4 | 150 | $\infty$ | 7 |
| B | 1 | 0 | 50 | 6 |
| B | 2 | 50 | 100 | 4 |
| B | 3 | 100 | $\infty$ | 3 |
| C | 1 | 0 | 100 | 5 |
| C | 2 | 100 | $\infty$ | 4 |

**Resource-implied upper bounds** $M_i$ (max producible of $i$ alone, given each resource):

- $M_A = \min\{\lfloor 100/1\rfloor, \lfloor 700/10\rfloor, \lfloor 400/3\rfloor\} = \min\{100, 70, 133\} = 70$
- $M_B = \min\{\lfloor 100/2\rfloor, \lfloor 700/4\rfloor, \lfloor 400/2\rfloor\} = \min\{50, 175, 200\} = 50$
- $M_C = \min\{\lfloor 100/1\rfloor, \lfloor 700/5\rfloor, \lfloor 400/1\rfloor\} = \min\{100, 140, 400\} = 100$

**Segment capacities** $\text{cap}_{ik}$ (last segment truncated at $M_i$):

$$\text{cap}_{ik} = U_{ik} - L_{ik} \text{ for } k < |K_i|, \qquad \text{cap}_{i,|K_i|} = M_i - L_{i,|K_i|}$$

| $i$ | $k$ | $L_{ik}$ | $U_{ik}$ | $\text{cap}_{ik}$ | $p_{ik}$ |
|-----|-----|----------|----------|-------------------|----------|
| A | 1 | 0 | 40 | 40 | 10 |
| A | 2 | 40 | 100 | 60 | 9 |
| A | 3 | 100 | 150 | 50 | 8 |
| A | 4 | 150 | — | $70-150=-80 \to 0$ | 7 |
| B | 1 | 0 | 50 | 50 | 6 |
| B | 2 | 50 | 100 | 50 | 4 |
| B | 3 | 100 | — | $50-100=-50 \to 0$ | 3 |
| C | 1 | 0 | 100 | 100 | 5 |
| C | 2 | 100 | — | $100-100=0$ | 4 |

(Where $M_i \le L_{ik}$, we set $\text{cap}_{ik}=0$; the segment is unreachable.)

## 3. Decision Variables

- $x_i \ge 0$ — total production (= sales) of product $i$
- $y_{ik} \ge 0$ — amount of product $i$ produced in segment $k$
- $z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if segment $k$ of product $i$ is used (opened)

## 4. Objective

$$\max \; \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K_i} p_{ik}\, y_{ik}$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Total production equals sum of segment amounts:**
$$x_i = \sum_{k\in K_i} y_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C2) Segment capacity linking:**
$$y_{ik} \le \text{cap}_{ik}\, z_{ik} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k\in K_i$$

**(C3) Monotonicity (fill-in-order):**
$$z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

**(C4) Resource constraints:**
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{tech}}\, x_i \le 100$$
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{labor}}\, x_i \le 700$$
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{mat}}\, x_i \le 400$$

**(C5) Domains:**
$$x_i \ge 0,\quad y_{ik} \ge 0,\quad z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}$$

## 6. Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Sales volume = production volume.** No inventory is carried and there is no separate demand cap; every unit produced is sold. Hence $x_i$ is both production and sales, and the objective sums profit over produced units only.
2. **Decreasing (concave) piecewise-constant unit profit.** Within each segment the unit profit $p_{ik}$ is constant, and $p_{i1} > p_{i2} > \dots$. This concavity is why the standard incremental formulation (C2)+(C3) is correct: the optimizer has no incentive to open a later (lower-profit) segment before an earlier one is full.
3. **Standard incremental formulation only.** We use monotonicity $z_{i,k+1}\le z_{ik}$ together with linking $y_{ik}\le \text{cap}_{ik} z_{ik}$. The redundant constraint $y_{ik}\ge (U_{ik}-L_{ik})z_{i,k+1}$ is **removed**; monotonicity + linking already enforce fill-in-order for a decreasing profit schedule.
4. **Unreachable segments retained for generality.** With $M_A=70$: segments A3 (100–150) and A4 (>150) are unreachable ($\text{cap}=0$ / $M_A<L$). With $M_B=50$: B2 (50–100) and B3 (>100) are unreachable. With $M_C=100$: C2 (>100) is unreachable. They remain in the model (with $\text{cap}=0$ where applicable) but will be zero in any feasible solution.
5. **LP relaxation already orders segments.** Because unit profits are decreasing (concave), the LP relaxation of (C1)–(C4) already fills segments in order; the binaries $z_{ik}$ are retained only for explicit ordering / generality (and would matter if the profit schedule were non-concave).
6. **Resource capacities:** tech 100, labor 700, material 400.

## 7. Compact Model Summary

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \;& \sum_{i}\sum_{k} p_{ik} y_{ik} \\
\text{s.t.}\;& x_i = \sum_{k} y_{ik} && \forall i\\
& y_{ik} \le \text{cap}_{ik}\, z_{ik} && \forall i,k\\
& z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i|\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{tech}} x_i \le 100\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{labor}} x_i \le 700\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{mat}} x_i \le 400\\
& x_i \ge 0,\; y_{ik}\ge 0,\; z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

With $\text{cap}$ values: $A:(40,60,50,0)$, $B:(50,0,0)$, $C:(100,0)$, and profits $A:(10,9,8,7)$, $B:(6,4,3)$, $C:(5,4)$.

- $M_C = \min(100/1,\; 700/5,\; 400/1) = \min(100, 140, 400) = 100$

**Important observation:** With these resource limits, product A can never exceed 70 units, so segments 3 and 4 of A are unreachable, and product C can never exceed 100 units, so segment 2 of C is unreachable. Product B can reach at most 50 units, so segments 2 and 3 of B are unreachable. To keep the model general and faithful to the stated schedule, we keep all segments but use $M_i$ as the upper bound in the last segment. - $x_i \ge 0$: total production of product $i$ (continuous).

### Segment variables
- $y_{ik} \ge 0$: quantity of product $i$ produced/sold **within segment $k$** (continuous).
- $z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if segment $k$ of product $i$ is "open" (has positive quantity), 0 otherwise.

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total profit:

$$\max \; Z = \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{k \in K_i} p_{ik}\, y_{ik}$$

Because unit profit is decreasing in $k$, and the ordering constraints below force segments to be filled in order, this correctly represents the piecewise-constant decreasing marginal profit.

## 5. Constraints

### (a) Total production equals sum of segment quantities

$$x_i = \sum_{k \in K_i} y_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

### (b) Segment capacity (linking $y$ and $z$)

$$y_{ik} \le (U_{ik} - L_{ik})\, z_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k \in K_i$$

(For the last segment, $U_{ik}-L_{ik}$ is replaced by $M_i - L_{ik}$.)

### (c) Ordering / fill-in-order constraints (SOS1-style)

Segment $k+1$ can only be used if segment $k$ is fully used:

$$y_{ik} \ge (U_{ik} - L_{ik})\, z_{i,k+1} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k = 1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

Equivalently, in binary form:

$$z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k = 1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

Using **both** (b) and (c) is the standard "incremental" piecewise-linear formulation; (c) ensures the decreasing price schedule is applied in order (you cannot use the cheaper higher-volume price before filling the lower-volume segment).

### (d) Resource capacity constraints

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{tech}}\, x_i \le 100$$

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{lab}}\, x_i \le 700$$

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{mat}}\, x_i \le 400$$

$$10\,x_A + 4\,x_B + 5\,x_C \le 700 \quad \text{(labor)}$$
$$3\,x_A + 2\,x_B + 1\,x_C \le 400 \quad \text{(material)}$$

### (e) Variable domains

$$x_i \ge 0, \quad y_{ik} \ge 0, \quad z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Complete Model (compact form)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = \sum_{i}\sum_{k} p_{ik} y_{ik} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_i = \sum_{k} y_{ik} && \forall i \\
& y_{ik} \le (U_{ik}-L_{ik})\, z_{ik} && \forall i,k \\
& y_{ik} \ge (U_{ik}-L_{ik})\, z_{i,k+1} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i| \\
& z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i| \\
& \sum_i r_{i,\text{tech}} x_i \le 100 \\
& \sum_i r_{i,\text{lab}} x_i \le 700 \\
& \sum_i r_{i,\text{mat}} x_i \le 400 \\
& x_i, y_{ik} \ge 0,\quad z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 7. Explanation of Modeling Choices and Assumptions

1. **Piecewise-constant decreasing profit.** The profit per unit is constant on each volume interval and decreases as volume grows. The objective $\sum p_{ik} y_{ik}$ with $y_{ik}$ the quantity in segment $k$ gives the exact total profit when segments are filled in order.

2. **Fill-in-order (convexity of the profit function).** Because $p_{ik}$ is *decreasing* in $k$, the profit function is concave in $x_i$. | $i$ | $k$ | $L_{ik}$ | $U_{ik}$ | $p_{ik}$ |
|-----|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| A | 1 | 0 | 40 | 10 |
| A | 2 | 40 | 100 | 9 |
| A | 3 | 100 | 150 | 8 |
| A | 4 | 150 | $\infty$ | 7 |
| B | 1 | 0 | 50 | 6 |
| B | 2 | 50 | 100 | 4 |
| B | 3 | 100 | $\infty$ | 3 |
| C | 1 | 0 | 100 | 5 |
| C | 2 | 100 | $\infty$ | 4 |

**Resource-implied upper bounds** $M_i$ (max producible of $i$ alone, given each resource):

- $M_A = \min\{\lfloor 100/1\rfloor, \lfloor 700/10\rfloor, \lfloor 400/3\rfloor\} = \min\{100, 70, 133\} = 70$
- $M_B = \min\{\lfloor 100/2\rfloor, \lfloor 700/4\rfloor, \lfloor 400/2\rfloor\} = \min\{50, 175, 200\} = 50$
- $M_C = \min\{\lfloor 100/1\rfloor, \lfloor 700/5\rfloor, \lfloor 400/1\rfloor\} = \min\{100, 140, 400\} = 100$

**Segment capacities** $\text{cap}_{ik}$ (last segment truncated at $M_i$):

$$\text{cap}_{ik} = U_{ik} - L_{ik} \text{ for } k < |K_i|, \qquad \text{cap}_{i,|K_i|} = M_i - L_{i,|K_i|}$$

| $i$ | $k$ | $L_{ik}$ | $U_{ik}$ | $\text{cap}_{ik}$ | $p_{ik}$ |
|-----|-----|----------|----------|-------------------|----------|
| A | 1 | 0 | 40 | 40 | 10 |
| A | 2 | 40 | 100 | 60 | 9 |
| A | 3 | 100 | 150 | 50 | 8 |
| A | 4 | 150 | — | $70-150=-80 \to 0$ | 7 |
| B | 1 | 0 | 50 | 50 | 6 |
| B | 2 | 50 | 100 | 50 | 4 |
| B | 3 | 100 | — | $50-100=-50 \to 0$ | 3 |
| C | 1 | 0 | 100 | 100 | 5 |
| C | 2 | 100 | — | $100-100=0$ | 4 |

(Where $M_i \le L_{ik}$, we set $\text{cap}_{ik}=0$; the segment is unreachable.)

- $y_{ik} \ge 0$ — amount of product $i$ produced in segment $k$

$$x_i = \sum_{k\in K_i} y_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C2) Segment capacity linking:**
$$y_{ik} \le \text{cap}_{ik}\, z_{ik} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k\in K_i$$

$$z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{tech}}\, x_i \le 100$$
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{labor}}\, x_i \le 700$$
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{mat}}\, x_i \le 400$$

**(C5) Domains:**
$$x_i \ge 0,\quad y_{ik} \ge 0,\quad z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}$$

## 6. Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Sales volume = production volume.** No inventory is carried and there is no separate demand cap; every unit produced is sold. Hence $x_i$ is both production and sales, and the objective sums profit over produced units only.
2. **Decreasing (concave) piecewise-constant unit profit.** Within each segment the unit profit $p_{ik}$ is constant, and $p_{i1} > p_{i2} > \dots$. 6. **Resource capacities:** tech 100, labor 700, material 400.

## 7. Compact Model Summary

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \;& \sum_{i}\sum_{k} p_{ik} y_{ik} \\
\text{s.t.}\;& x_i = \sum_{k} y_{ik} && \forall i\\
& y_{ik} \le \text{cap}_{ik}\, z_{ik} && \forall i,k\\
& z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i|\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{tech}} x_i \le 100\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{labor}} x_i \le 700\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{mat}} x_i \le 400\\
& x_i \ge 0,\; y_{ik}\ge 0,\; z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

With $\text{cap}$ values: $A:(40,60,50,0)$, $B:(50,0,0)$, $C:(100,0)$, and profits $A:(10,9,8,7)$, $B:(6,4,3)$, $C:(5,4)$.

messages.content:
# MILP Formulation: Production Planning with Quantity-Discount Profit

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $i \in I = \{A, B, C\}$ | Products |
| $k \in K_i$ | Price segments for product $i$ (ordered from lowest to highest volume) |

Segment definitions:

- $K_A = \{1,2,3,4\}$, $K_B = \{1,2,3\}$, $K_C = \{1,2\}$

## 2. Parameters

### Resource coefficients $r_{i,\ell}$ (per unit of product $i$)

| Product | Tech. prep (h) | Labor (h) | Material (kg) |
|---------|---------------|-----------|---------------|
| A | 1 | 10 | 3 |
| B | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| C | 1 | 5 | 1 |

### Resource availability $R_\ell$

- Technical preparation: $R_{\text{tech}} = 100$
- Labor: $R_{\text{lab}} = 700$
- Material: $R_{\text{mat}} = 400$

### Segment bounds and unit profits

For each product $i$ and segment $k$, let $[L_{ik}, U_{ik}]$ be the volume interval and $p_{ik}$ the unit profit (constant within the segment):

**Product A** ($p_{A,k}$ decreasing):

| $k$ | $L_{Ak}$ | $U_{Ak}$ | $p_{Ak}$ |
|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| 1 | 0 | 40 | 10 |
| 2 | 40 | 100 | 9 |
| 3 | 100 | 150 | 8 |
| 4 | 150 | $\infty$ (use big-$M$) | 7 |

**Product B**:

| $k$ | $L_{Bk}$ | $U_{Bk}$ | $p_{Bk}$ |
|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| 1 | 0 | 50 | 6 |
| 2 | 50 | 100 | 4 |
| 3 | 100 | $\infty$ | 3 |

**Product C**:

| $k$ | $L_{Ck}$ | $U_{Ck}$ | $p_{Ck}$ |
|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| 1 | 0 | 100 | 5 |
| 2 | 100 | $\infty$ | 4 |

### Big-$M$ values

Choose $M_i$ = an upper bound on production of product $i$ implied by resources:

- $M_A = \min(100/1,\; 700/10,\; 400/3) = \min(100, 70, 133.3) = 70$
- $M_B = \min(100/2,\; 700/4,\; 400/2) = \min(50, 175, 200) = 50$
- $M_C = \min(100/1,\; 700/5,\; 400/1) = \min(100, 140, 400) = 100$

**Important observation:** With these resource limits, product A can never exceed 70 units, so segments 3 and 4 of A are unreachable, and product C can never exceed 100 units, so segment 2 of C is unreachable. Product B can reach at most 50 units, so segments 2 and 3 of B are unreachable. To keep the model general and faithful to the stated schedule, we keep all segments but use $M_i$ as the upper bound in the last segment. (In practice you could drop unreachable segments; the model below remains correct either way.)

## 3. Decision Variables

### Production quantities
- $x_i \ge 0$: total production of product $i$ (continuous).

### Segment variables
- $y_{ik} \ge 0$: quantity of product $i$ produced/sold **within segment $k$** (continuous).
- $z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if segment $k$ of product $i$ is "open" (has positive quantity), 0 otherwise.

## 4. Objective Function

Maximize total profit:

$$\max \; Z = \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{k \in K_i} p_{ik}\, y_{ik}$$

Because unit profit is decreasing in $k$, and the ordering constraints below force segments to be filled in order, this correctly represents the piecewise-constant decreasing marginal profit.

## 5. Constraints

### (a) Total production equals sum of segment quantities

$$x_i = \sum_{k \in K_i} y_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

### (b) Segment capacity (linking $y$ and $z$)

$$y_{ik} \le (U_{ik} - L_{ik})\, z_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k \in K_i$$

(For the last segment, $U_{ik}-L_{ik}$ is replaced by $M_i - L_{ik}$.)

### (c) Ordering / fill-in-order constraints (SOS1-style)

Segment $k+1$ can only be used if segment $k$ is fully used:

$$y_{ik} \ge (U_{ik} - L_{ik})\, z_{i,k+1} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k = 1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

Equivalently, in binary form:

$$z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I,\; k = 1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

Using **both** (b) and (c) is the standard "incremental" piecewise-linear formulation; (c) ensures the decreasing price schedule is applied in order (you cannot use the cheaper higher-volume price before filling the lower-volume segment).

> **Note on the first segment:** For $k=1$, $L_{i1}=0$, so (b) reads $y_{i1} \le U_{i1} z_{i1}$. The constraint (c) for $k=1$ is $y_{i1} \ge U_{i1} z_{i2}$, which forces segment 1 to be full before segment 2 opens. This is the correct "fill in order" condition.

### (d) Resource capacity constraints

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{tech}}\, x_i \le 100$$

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{lab}}\, x_i \le 700$$

$$\sum_{i \in I} r_{i,\text{mat}}\, x_i \le 400$$

Explicitly:

$$1\,x_A + 2\,x_B + 1\,x_C \le 100 \quad \text{(technical preparation)}$$
$$10\,x_A + 4\,x_B + 5\,x_C \le 700 \quad \text{(labor)}$$
$$3\,x_A + 2\,x_B + 1\,x_C \le 400 \quad \text{(material)}$$

### (e) Variable domains

$$x_i \ge 0, \quad y_{ik} \ge 0, \quad z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Complete Model (compact form)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & Z = \sum_{i}\sum_{k} p_{ik} y_{ik} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad
& x_i = \sum_{k} y_{ik} && \forall i \\
& y_{ik} \le (U_{ik}-L_{ik})\, z_{ik} && \forall i,k \\
& y_{ik} \ge (U_{ik}-L_{ik})\, z_{i,k+1} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i| \\
& z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i| \\
& \sum_i r_{i,\text{tech}} x_i \le 100 \\
& \sum_i r_{i,\text{lab}} x_i \le 700 \\
& \sum_i r_{i,\text{mat}} x_i \le 400 \\
& x_i, y_{ik} \ge 0,\quad z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 7. Explanation of Modeling Choices and Assumptions

1. **Piecewise-constant decreasing profit.** The profit per unit is constant on each volume interval and decreases as volume grows. The objective $\sum p_{ik} y_{ik}$ with $y_{ik}$ the quantity in segment $k$ gives the exact total profit when segments are filled in order.

2. **Fill-in-order (convexity of the profit function).** Because $p_{ik}$ is *decreasing* in $k$, the profit function is concave in $x_i$. For a concave piecewise-linear function, the LP relaxation automatically fills segments in order, so the binaries are not strictly needed for correctness of the optimum — but they are included (as requested) to make the ordering explicit and to keep the model valid even if the schedule were non-concave. The constraints (b)+(c) enforce: segment $k+1$ can carry positive quantity only if segment $k$ is at its upper bound.

3. **Upper bounds / big-$M$.** The last segment of each product is unbounded above in the problem statement; we cap it at $M_i$, a valid production upper bound derived from the tightest resource. This keeps the MILP bounded without changing the feasible region (since resources already imply $x_i \le M_i$).

4. **Continuous quantities.** $x_i$ and $y_{ik}$ are continuous (units may be fractional), as stated. Only the segment-opening indicators $z_{ik}$ are binary.

5. **No inventory, no demand cap.** All production is sold within the period; the only limits are resources. There is no separate demand constraint, so the "sales volume" equals production volume.

6. **Unreachable segments.** Given the resource limits, some segments (A3, A4, B2, B3, C2) can never be entered. They are retained for generality; a solver will simply set their $z_{ik}=0$. You may delete them to reduce model size.

7. **SOS1 alternative.** Instead of constraints (b)–(c), one could declare $\{y_{i1},\dots,y_{i,|K_i|}\}$ as an SOS1 set with the convention that the "active" variable is the marginal one; the incremental formulation above is equivalent and more standard for MILP solvers.

# Feedback on the Generated Model

The model is mostly correct, but I identified several issues to fix:

1. **Redundant/over-constrained ordering.** Using *both* linking constraints (b) and the fill-in-order constraint (c) in the form `y_{ik} ≥ (U_{ik}−L_{ik})·z_{i,k+1}` is problematic: it forces segment k to be *exactly full* whenever segment k+1 is open, which is fine, but combined with the monotonicity `z_{i,k+1} ≤ z_{ik}` it double-enforces. More importantly, mixing the two is redundant and can create numerical issues. The clean standard incremental formulation should use **only** the monotonicity `z_{i,k+1} ≤ z_{ik}` plus the linking `y_{ik} ≤ cap_{ik}·z_{ik}`.

2. **Big-M for last segment.** The last segment capacity must be `M_i − L_{i,last}`, not `M_i`, and this must be stated explicitly per product.

3. **Unreachable segments should be flagged but kept** — good, but the model should note that `M_A = 70` makes A3/A4 impossible, so the *effective* schedule is truncated. This is a modeling assumption worth stating clearly.

4. **Missing explicit statement that sales = production** and no inventory — present but should be prominent.

5. **Objective correctness check:** since profits are decreasing (concave), the LP relaxation already fills in order; binaries are only needed for generality. Keep them but note this.

Let me have the or_operator revise with these corrections.

# Corrected MILP: Production Planning with Decreasing Piecewise-Constant Unit Profit

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $i \in I = \{A, B, C\}$ — products
- $k \in K_i$ — profit segments for product $i$:
  - $K_A = \{1,2,3,4\}$, $K_B = \{1,2,3\}$, $K_C = \{1,2\}$
- $r \in R = \{\text{tech}, \text{labor}, \text{mat}\}$ — resources

## 2. Parameters

**Resource consumption per unit** $a_{ir}$:

| $i$ | tech | labor | mat |
|-----|------|-------|-----|
| A | 1 | 10 | 3 |
| B | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| C | 1 | 5 | 1 |

**Resource capacities** $b_r$: $b_{\text{tech}} = 100$, $b_{\text{labor}} = 700$, $b_{\text{mat}} = 400$.

**Segment breakpoints** $L_{ik}$, $U_{ik}$ and **unit profits** $p_{ik}$:

| $i$ | $k$ | $L_{ik}$ | $U_{ik}$ | $p_{ik}$ |
|-----|-----|----------|----------|----------|
| A | 1 | 0 | 40 | 10 |
| A | 2 | 40 | 100 | 9 |
| A | 3 | 100 | 150 | 8 |
| A | 4 | 150 | $\infty$ | 7 |
| B | 1 | 0 | 50 | 6 |
| B | 2 | 50 | 100 | 4 |
| B | 3 | 100 | $\infty$ | 3 |
| C | 1 | 0 | 100 | 5 |
| C | 2 | 100 | $\infty$ | 4 |

**Resource-implied upper bounds** $M_i$ (max producible of $i$ alone, given each resource):

- $M_A = \min\{\lfloor 100/1\rfloor, \lfloor 700/10\rfloor, \lfloor 400/3\rfloor\} = \min\{100, 70, 133\} = 70$
- $M_B = \min\{\lfloor 100/2\rfloor, \lfloor 700/4\rfloor, \lfloor 400/2\rfloor\} = \min\{50, 175, 200\} = 50$
- $M_C = \min\{\lfloor 100/1\rfloor, \lfloor 700/5\rfloor, \lfloor 400/1\rfloor\} = \min\{100, 140, 400\} = 100$

**Segment capacities** $\text{cap}_{ik}$ (last segment truncated at $M_i$):

$$\text{cap}_{ik} = U_{ik} - L_{ik} \text{ for } k < |K_i|, \qquad \text{cap}_{i,|K_i|} = M_i - L_{i,|K_i|}$$

| $i$ | $k$ | $L_{ik}$ | $U_{ik}$ | $\text{cap}_{ik}$ | $p_{ik}$ |
|-----|-----|----------|----------|-------------------|----------|
| A | 1 | 0 | 40 | 40 | 10 |
| A | 2 | 40 | 100 | 60 | 9 |
| A | 3 | 100 | 150 | 50 | 8 |
| A | 4 | 150 | — | $70-150=-80 \to 0$ | 7 |
| B | 1 | 0 | 50 | 50 | 6 |
| B | 2 | 50 | 100 | 50 | 4 |
| B | 3 | 100 | — | $50-100=-50 \to 0$ | 3 |
| C | 1 | 0 | 100 | 100 | 5 |
| C | 2 | 100 | — | $100-100=0$ | 4 |

(Where $M_i \le L_{ik}$, we set $\text{cap}_{ik}=0$; the segment is unreachable.)

## 3. Decision Variables

- $x_i \ge 0$ — total production (= sales) of product $i$
- $y_{ik} \ge 0$ — amount of product $i$ produced in segment $k$
- $z_{ik} \in \{0,1\}$ — 1 if segment $k$ of product $i$ is used (opened)

## 4. Objective

$$\max \; \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K_i} p_{ik}\, y_{ik}$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Total production equals sum of segment amounts:**
$$x_i = \sum_{k\in K_i} y_{ik} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C2) Segment capacity linking:**
$$y_{ik} \le \text{cap}_{ik}\, z_{ik} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k\in K_i$$

**(C3) Monotonicity (fill-in-order):**
$$z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1$$

**(C4) Resource constraints:**
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{tech}}\, x_i \le 100$$
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{labor}}\, x_i \le 700$$
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_{i,\text{mat}}\, x_i \le 400$$

**(C5) Domains:**
$$x_i \ge 0,\quad y_{ik} \ge 0,\quad z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}$$

## 6. Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Sales volume = production volume.** No inventory is carried and there is no separate demand cap; every unit produced is sold. Hence $x_i$ is both production and sales, and the objective sums profit over produced units only.
2. **Decreasing (concave) piecewise-constant unit profit.** Within each segment the unit profit $p_{ik}$ is constant, and $p_{i1} > p_{i2} > \dots$. This concavity is why the standard incremental formulation (C2)+(C3) is correct: the optimizer has no incentive to open a later (lower-profit) segment before an earlier one is full.
3. **Standard incremental formulation only.** We use monotonicity $z_{i,k+1}\le z_{ik}$ together with linking $y_{ik}\le \text{cap}_{ik} z_{ik}$. The redundant constraint $y_{ik}\ge (U_{ik}-L_{ik})z_{i,k+1}$ is **removed**; monotonicity + linking already enforce fill-in-order for a decreasing profit schedule.
4. **Unreachable segments retained for generality.** With $M_A=70$: segments A3 (100–150) and A4 (>150) are unreachable ($\text{cap}=0$ / $M_A<L$). With $M_B=50$: B2 (50–100) and B3 (>100) are unreachable. With $M_C=100$: C2 (>100) is unreachable. They remain in the model (with $\text{cap}=0$ where applicable) but will be zero in any feasible solution.
5. **LP relaxation already orders segments.** Because unit profits are decreasing (concave), the LP relaxation of (C1)–(C4) already fills segments in order; the binaries $z_{ik}$ are retained only for explicit ordering / generality (and would matter if the profit schedule were non-concave).
6. **Resource capacities:** tech 100, labor 700, material 400.

## 7. Compact Model Summary

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \;& \sum_{i}\sum_{k} p_{ik} y_{ik} \\
\text{s.t.}\;& x_i = \sum_{k} y_{ik} && \forall i\\
& y_{ik} \le \text{cap}_{ik}\, z_{ik} && \forall i,k\\
& z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} && \forall i,\; k<|K_i|\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{tech}} x_i \le 100\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{labor}} x_i \le 700\\
& \textstyle\sum_i a_{i,\text{mat}} x_i \le 400\\
& x_i \ge 0,\; y_{ik}\ge 0,\; z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

With $\text{cap}$ values: $A:(40,60,50,0)$, $B:(50,0,0)$, $C:(100,0)$, and profits $A:(10,9,8,7)$, $B:(6,4,3)$, $C:(5,4)$.

& z_{i,k+1} \le z_{ik} && \forall i,\; k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1 \quad\text{(C3: fill-in-order)}\\
& x_A + 2x_B + x_C \le 100 && \text{(C4: technical preparation)}\\
& 10x_A + 4x_B + 5x_C \le 700 && \text{(C5: labor)}\\
& 3x_A + 2x_B + x_C \le 400 && \text{(C6: material)}\\
& x_i\ge 0,\; y_{ik}\ge 0,\; z_{ik}\in\{0,1\} && \text{(C7: domains)}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Sales = production.** No inventory, no separate demand cap; every unit produced is sold, so $x_i$ is both production and sales.
2. **Decreasing (concave) unit profit.** $p_{i1}>p_{i2}>\dots$ within each product; the incremental formulation (C2)+(C3) correctly fills segments in order.
3. **Standard incremental form only.** Monotonicity (C3) plus linking (C2) enforce ordering; no redundant lower-bound constraint is used.

5. **LP relaxation already orders segments** (concavity); binaries are retained for explicit ordering and generality.
6. **Continuous quantities** (units may be fractional); only $z_{ik}$ are binary.
